speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY TABLING OF NOTES EXCHANGED BETWEEN THE UNITED STATES AND CANADA
speechtext:
I should like to table two copies in English and two copies in French of notes exchanged between the United States ambassador to Canada and myself, on June 7 and June 16, respectively, on the subject of the St. Lawrence seaway.
Hon. members will see from these notes that the United States government, in transmitting copies of the Wiley Act recently adopted by congress, stated that it was anxious to undertake discussions with the Canadian government on the subject of the seaway. Canada is prepared to do so at the earliest date convenient to both governments.
Because it may not be very clear why discussions between the two governments should be held at this time, it might be useful for me to add a few words of explanation. In 1951, the Canadian parliament enacted the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act which allows a Canadian corporation to build the seaway from lake Erie to the port of Montreal in Canadian territory. By exchange of notes dated June 30, 1952, and tabled in parliament on July 1, 1952, Canada and the United States agreed that the power project in the international rapids section should be built jointly by Canada and the United States and that this project should be separated, as far as is possible, from the seaway project. As for the seaway project, the exchange of notes of June 30, 1952,
between Canada and the United States embodied an arrangement whereby Canada would build the seaway between lake Erie and the port of Montreal on its side of the boundary. This was, of course, before the passage of the Wiley Act which provided for United States participation.
With the passage of the Wiley Act, the situation could be summed up as follows: Canada is fully empowered by its own legislation to build the seaway from lake Erie to Montreal; an international agreement or arrangement between Canada and the United States has recorded the agreement of both countries to this course of action. However, hon. members will recall that as far back as January 9, 1953, and as late as May 6, 1954, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) declared that the Canadian government was prepared to discuss any specific proposal which the United States government might wish to make, the sense of which would be to vary that portion of the arrangements of June 30, 1952, dealing with the seaway, provided no delay would be caused in the construction of the seaway or power projects, as a result of the consideration of such proposal. Finally, the congress of the United States decided, in May 1954, to build a segment of this seaway entirely within United States territory. Clearly, then, if the object of the Wiley Act is to be achieved, it becomes necessary to hold discussions between Canada and the United States in order to modify the existing arrangements between the governments as contained in the notes of June 30, 1952.
Because of the nature of the arrangements of June 30, 1952, and of undertakings given by Canada, talks must be undertaken soon if they are not to delay the seaway or power projects. Canada accordingly suggested on June 16 that discussions between officials of both governments be held in Ottawa in the week of June 28, for the purpose of preparing specific topics which might form the basis for subsequent intergovernmental discussions. I have not heard yet from the United States ambassador what exact date would be agreeable to his government, but I expect that the talks will get under way in Ottawa in the very near future.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY TABLING OF NOTES EXCHANGED BETWEEN THE UNITED STATES AND CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words about this but with particular reference to one source of satisfaction which

St. Lawrence Seaway
I feel should be in the mind of every hon. member and every Canadian, that we have reached the point when talks of this kind can take place. Very naturally there has been great emphasis upon the opportunity for larger ships to pass up and down the St. Lawrence to the upper waters of our great inland waterways. Naturally also great emphasis has been placed upon the much needed and immense resources of electric energy which will become available.
I am inclined to think, however, that perhaps one of the most valuable features of the undertaking which is contemplated by this conference is the unique evidence which will be given not merely of our verbal and very real expressions of understanding between Canada and the United States, but of one of the most remarkable and practical examples of international co-operation the world has ever seen, and I am not aware of any similar undertaking along the boundary of any other two nations. As we see that waterway go ahead, as we see the power development take place and the greatly needed horsepower become available for industry and for the farms and homes of this province as well as New York state, let us thank God that two nations can live together, work together, and understand each other as these two nations do.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY TABLING OF NOTES EXCHANGED BETWEEN THE UNITED STATES AND CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say that up to a certain point I agree with what the Leader of the Opposition has said. As I have said in this house before, I think that under certain foreseeable circumstances it might be better if one or the other of the two countries undertook this project of its own volition. I believe that would prevent any complications in the future. However, discussions are to take place with regard to a joint undertaking. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the government will carry out the pledge given that this co-operation and the preparation for it must involve no unnecessary delay. We have had so many years of discussion about this project that if there is any disposition to delay I think the matter should be proceeded with by Canada. We have the legislation and the government has the authority, and I think the project should be proceeded with by Canada alone if necessary.
I agree with the Leader of the Opposition, however, that the demonstration of the undertaking of a power project on a joint basis is sufficient evidence to the world that two nations can live together side by side with a contiguous boundary and be able to undertake a joint project of this description. However, I hope there will be no delay, and if there is any disposition to delay I hope the government will proceed to build this as a

Canadian project; because, as I have already said and I would like to emphasize this, I think that for the future it would be better if one or other of the two governments undertook this project of its own volition, and X would have liked to have seen Canada undertake this project in that way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make a short statement on this matter yesterday, but I thought it would be courteous for me to wait until the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who asked the original question, was in his place. I can say now, as I would have said yesterday, that there is not enough information to give any adequate or final answer to the questions that have been asked.
The political situation in regard to developments in Guatemala is certainly not clear, though the military position would appear, on the information at our disposal, to be reaching a climax. To the best of my knowledge, based on information we have received, the attacking forces in Guatemala seem to be Guatemalan, though some non-Guatemalans may be included in those forces.
As hon. members know, the United Nations has intervened. A meeting of the security council was requested by the Guatemalan government, and it was held, immediately after their request, last Sunday. At that meeting representatives of Guatemala alleged invasion and aggression by "foreign mercenaries", but made no charges against any other country, neighbouring or otherwise. Thereupon the delegates of Brazil and Colombia introduced a resolution at the security council to submit the question urgently to the Organization of American States. That resolution was approved by a majority but was vetoed by the delegate of the Soviet union. Thereupon the delegate of France introduced a resolution calling for the immediate termination of any action likely to cause bloodshed, and requesting all members of the United Nations to refrain from giving assistance to any such action. That resolution was carried unanimously.
We have received messages direct from Guatemala from the Canadian government trade commissioner in that city, and he has told us that the lives and property of Canadian citizens were not at that time in any danger. A later message received yesterday afternoon indicated that matters would be reaching a climax very shortly indeed. Apart from the trade commissioner and his 83276-412
Inquiries of the Ministry family, there are, as far as we know, about 24 Canadian residents in Guatemala.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish merely to make a comment in relation to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) because it does suggest that perhaps a good deal of caution should be exercised in approaching this subject. I was extremely interested when I received last Saturday morning a letter from the secretary of the communist party in Canada urging that, along with other believers in democracy, we should assert our views with regard to the Guatemalan situation. I was extremely interested in the speed with which the party line had been declared and duly indicated by the servants of Moscow here in Canada. I wish to make this perfectly clear: I am not for one moment suggesting that any question -and very proper questions they were- devoted to this subject should not be asked. I cannot, however, refrain from expressing my interest in the promptness with which our communists here in this country follow the party line and the orders from Moscow. I propose to keep with some interest that communication received only the day after the trouble started in Guatemala, as evidence at least of the efficiency of this world treachery.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct to the Minister of Labour a question of which I have given him notice: Has there been any change by regulation or otherwise in the interpretation of section 41 of the Unemployment Insurance Act-disqualification for benefits- in the case of a stoppage of work due to a labour dispute where only a small classified group of the main bargaining unit withdraws its labour from the service of the employer;

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Inquiries of the Ministry and what is the position under the act of the main body of workers in the bargaining unit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for giving me notice of his question. In reply to the first part of it, I can tell him that there has been no change. In reply to the second part, I do not think I can do better than to quote part of section 41 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which reads as follows:
41. (1) An insured person is disqualified from receiving benefit if he has lost his employment by reason of a stoppage of work due to a labour dispute at the factory, workshop or other premises at which he was employed unless he has, during the stoppage of work, become bona fide employed elsewhere in the occupation that he usually follows, or has become regularly engaged in some other occupation; but this disqualification lasts only so long as the stoppage of work continues.
(2) An insured person is not disqualified under this section if he proves
(a)	that he is not participating in, or financing or directly interested in the labour dispute that caused the stoppage of work, and
(b)	that he does not belong to a grade or class of workers of which immediately before the commencement of the stoppage there were members employed at the premises at which the stoppage is taking place any of whom are participating in, financing or directly interested in the dispute.
To that I would add that in a decision in 1951 the Canadian umpire, who is the final authority under our Unemployment Insurance Act, said as follows:
I readily endorse the following remarks made by the British umpire: "It seems to me that the intention of the act is to exclude from benefits, in addition to the workers who are directly interested, those who are indirectly interested by reason of the terms and conditions of their employment being the same as the persons who are directly interested".
In a number of decisions the Canadian umpire has maintained the principle set out in his 1951 decision from which I have just quoted. I would draw the attention of the hon. member to decisions-C.U.B. 981-1019- of the umpire, copies of which are available. I can send them to him if he wishes me to do so.

When I noticed this report, Mr. Speaker, I naturally caused inquiries to be made, and I received from General Simonds a telegram explaining the circumstances of his statement and also stating more fully and perhaps more accurately what he said. He was at a meeting of officers of the Canadian Army in Saint John, New Brunswick, and after a talk he gave them he was asked a question which is quite frequently put on similar occasions. I myself have been asked it a great number of times. He was asked what his views were on the subject of national service. He made a reply which I think you could expect almost any officer to make, namely that he would be glad to see every youth in the country receive two years' military training. Then he went on to say:
I believe the vast majority of experienced soldiers would agree with me. But such training was impossible unless it received the wholehearted support of the people of this country and that was a matter for judgment and decision by political leaders, not soldiers. In any event experience tended to show that a period of universal military service of less than two years increased rather than diminished the problem of meeting commitment overseas. Further a system of universal military 83276-412J
Supply-Privy Council service was not a substitution for voluntary service, it could only supplement and never replace the voluntary system.

I merely asked the question in view of the fact that I have certain comments to make and wished to know whether the Prime Minister intended to say anything. It does seem to me that on this first item of the privy council estimates it is appropriate to mention certain subjects which are of concern to all of us and in regard to which the Prime Minister of necessity under our system must assume responsibility. I propose to direct my remarks to four particular subjects that it seems to me have emerged as extremely important subjects during the course of the present session.
I now wish to place these before the Prime Minister at this stage of the session in view of the fact that it is within his power to deal with them while the house is not in session. Moreover, I believe these things are things which should be dealt with before we meet again some time later this year. The first of these subjects is the business of parliament itself; the second is the judiciary; the third, a conference between federal and provincial governments; and the fourth a commonwealth conference. It is to those subjects that I propose to address my remarks because of my belief that all of them are subjects that can be, and under our system must be, dealt with upon the responsibility of the government itself. I have no intention of reviewing the extended comments there have been on different occasions about the business of the house during the present session, beyond such reference as it seems to me is appropriate to emphasize my belief that much can be done between now and the time we meet again to assure that we shall not have another session such as that which is now drawing to a close.

I know that there may be little occasion to emphasize the role of the prime minister under our parliamentary system. Sometimes, however, it does seem that even in this House of Commons there is a tendency to disregard the fact that the position of prime minister under our parliamentary system and similar parliamentary systems within the commonwealth is very different from that of a prime minister under any other system or even the head of state under a republican system. In Canada, in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand or any of the nations of the commonwealth, in Asia or in other parts of the world, the prime minister has a measure of power and authority which has led some writers to speak of the position as a democratic dictatorship.
I refer to that description, used in textbooks which express complete approval of our system, with no suggestion of criticism but rather merely to emphasize the extent of the authority that is conferred upon the prime minister under our system. He is the individual called upon by the representative of the queen or the king, as the case may be, at any given time in the history of our system to form a government. Within this country we have had the good fortune to have nearly always a clear and satisfactory majority on one side or the other. In a country where the responsibility of office has been shared for almost an equal number of years by two parties, and only two parties, it has contributed greatly to the maintenance of our system that we have not found ourselves dependent upon an uncertain association of parties without a common purpose.
Where there is a clear party majority, no matter what may be said about the large majority on this occasion, the fact remains that as long as there is a working majority the result is very similar in any event. The government takes the responsibility for initiating legislation. The government rides or falls upon the confidence of parliament expressed in the legislation to which the government commits itself. Therefore any prime minister must of necessity be very careful to consult the sentiment of the members of his own party after having carefully canvassed the sentiment of the cabinet in the first instance. That is the strength of our system. That can also be the weakness of our system if the authority and power conferred in that way are not exercised in the manner that will produce the best results from both the administrative and the legislative points of view.
I come back to the position of prime minister. Having been called upon to form a government, he names the members of the
[Mr. Drew.l

cabinet. To that extent it is definitely a government of his choice. There are historic cases where prime ministers in other countries decided to have a general consultation respecting the composition of the cabinet with some disastrous results, as all students of constitutional history will recall. From that point on the prime minister by virtue of his office has, under our parliamentary system, a unique responsibility not only for legislation, for what is done, but also for the business of parliament itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope we can be regular in our debates, and I know from former occasions it has been desirable to let hon. members make their speeches rather than to interrupt them. However, 1 did not make that answer. The committee has not finalized its recommendations, and what the committee may decide to do I do not know, being only one of 21 members.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have no desire to conduct a debate at arm's length with the minister, but I understood him to say there would be no report on the rule changes because some members on the other side did not wish it done. I took his words to mean exactly what they said. In fact, I was rather pleased that this was one of the first occasions upon which the views of the opposition were being accorded some recognition.
We can dispose of that, however, because the chairman has said that a general discussion is quite proper. I am pointing out that the speed with which we are able to proceed at the next session will depend upon what is done between now and the beginning of the next session. It is to that I am now directing these remarks. When the session begins, there will be a speech from the throne, as there was at the beginning of this and every other session. The speech from the throne, prepared by Her Majesty's advisers, is in fact a statement by the government of the business it intends to present to parliament. It is a guide to the members and to the public, as to what the government has already decided to do. It is a guide to the members on the other side of the house as to those things which they should try to bring forward if they feel there are subjects which are not otherwise going to be presented.
Since the government in that speech from the throne is stating what it proposes to do, then presumably before that statement is made a decision has already been made in

Supply-Privy Council cabinet in regard to each of these matters. In fact, it is not conceivable that any such statement would be made without a decision in advance by the cabinet. After that decision has been made by the cabinet, then in the ordinary course of events the legislation which is announced in the speech from the throne can be prepared in advance. In fact, unless it has been prepared in something approximating draft form it is difficult to understand how the cabinet could have given approval to the general idea. It is a matter of common knowledge that when any cabinet decides that a certain thing is going to be done, it does so upon the basis of a memorandum which substantially sets out what is contemplated in the form of legislation.
For that very reason, there can be no difficulty whatever in having most of the legislation ready at the time the session meets. Within a few days of the speech from the throne being read by Her Majesty's representative, a substantial part of the legislation could be put on the order paper. If that were done, then hon. members on both sides of the house would have the opportunity to examine that legislation, to avail themselves of the opportunities that are afforded for inquiry from people who are experts in the various fields, and to know in advance what it is that is to be considered.
Let us take just one example. For many weeks-I am inclined to think it is perhaps for some three months-we have been under the impression that legislation was to come forward to deal with amendments to judges' salaries. We were told that there was to be an amendment to the Judges Act. I believe that answer was given in response to a question I directed to the Prime Minister some time ago.
Even before that, however, there have been comments in the press about the likelihood of this taking place; and in this case the comments were shown to be well informed. However, the legislation that actually came down was not legislation of the kind contemplated. It will be recalled by hon. members that I have asked on different occasions if the Prime Minister would inform us in regard to the nature of the legislation, or when we might expect it; and, without attempting to give the exact words, the information received was that the government was not ready to give us this information.
Because it was thought that a measure dealing with judges' salaries was under consideration-incidentally, I might say it was known that consultation was taking place in regard to this subject between the government of Canada and representatives of at

least some of the provincial governments- hon. members did not raise this subject by way of a substantive motion, or otherwise.
Now we find that the amendment to the Judges Act is not an amendment such as had been contemplated by many members, but is an amendment which calls for the appointment of two new judges, one to the superior -court of Alberta and the other to the superior court of British Columbia. Without in any way considering the merits or the details of this subject, at least it can be said that hon. members were under the impression that the subject of judges' salaries was going to come forward.
Then, without any suggestion of raising another subject that, at least outside this house, might offer some possibility for extended argument, there is the fact that from the very time we heard the speech from the throne we were told that there was going to be an amendment to the Municipal Grants Act. For that very reason, substantive motions which we have presented on other occasions in regard to relief of the municipalities from certain taxes, and assessments on property, were not presented because we knew it had been stated that on the order paper there was going to be a resolution referring to the question of assistance to the municipalities.
Now we find, at this stage of the session, that the act is not going to be proceeded with. On the one hand we have the statement in the speech from the throne that an amendment was going to be presented-and, after all, that is a subject that must have been decided on, one way or another. It is a bill which surely should have been prepared. Not only do we not have the opportunity to deal with that act but, by virtue of the fact that a resolution has been on the order paper relating to it, we have been denied the opportunity to have other discussion take place which could have produced results.
When I made the comment I did make a short time ago in regard to members of the opposition being heard, may I say there have been occasions-and I certainly commend those ministers who have accepted these opportunities-to make various amendments on the basis of proposals which -came from the opposition. I can recall an amendment accepted by the Minister of Justice, and another amendment accepted by the minister of the new department which deals with northern affairs. I recall an amendment accepted by the Minister of National Revenue, as well as amendments accepted by other ministers. These were accepted in good spirit, as constructive suggestions which the government felt might improve the legislation they were presenting.

This is an indication of the value of having an early opportunity to consider legislation and to discuss it with those who can give sound advice. It would seem to me that well over half-perhaps three-quarters-of the legislation that would come forward in a session could be on the order paper within the first two weeks. After all, most of the bills are short, interpreting decisions already made by the government when the speech from the throne is prepared.
If those were on the order paper, particularly at the time we meet before Christmas, then during the extended Christmas holidays hon. members, who do take these tasks seriously-and the discussion that takes place indicates just how seriously they accept their responsibilities-would then come back with information that would make it possible to deal with these subjects much more rapidly.
Moreover, I am convinced that, if legislation were brought forward in this way, the debate on the speech from the throne would be greatly shortened. Hon. members would know what subjects were going to come up, and what the nature of the discussions would be within the framework of legislation they had already seen. For the same reason, the debate on the budget would be greatly shortened. This undoubtedly would encourage the direction of debate to positive measures before the house either by way of bills or by resolution.
Therefore in the light of what has happened during a session which is, at least, the second longest in Canadian history, and the least productive-
The third longest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am informed that only the session of 1903 was longer. However, whether it is the second or the third longest, may I say that this is certainly the longest of any session which has produced very little of a positive nature, with the exception of the amendments to the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

Hon. members have had to seek information by every device possible. We all know even within the last few days how rigidly the government refuses to open doors to information which is not confidential, by any ordinary meaning of the word, but which would have helped greatly to expedite the business of the house.

We do know that one of the departments, which proceeds most rapidly once its estimates come before the house, is the Department of External Affairs. And that is because, by custom, those estimates are referred to a committee, and dealt with there. When they come back to the house, hon. members know that representatives from both sides of the house have examined the items; and therefore, subject to such general debate as may take place in regard to external affairs, the house proceeds to deal with the estimates very quickly. I feel therefore that the same practice could be employed with very great advantage in the case of the Department of National Defence, in the case of the Department of Labour and in the case of other departments which naturally require some examination if the business is to be done expeditiously.
I recognize, Mr. Chairman, that there are always measures which cannot be ready when the house meets. I recognize that in this session there was a tremendous undertaking carried out by hon. members and by the other place in the amendment of the Criminal Code. The Minister of Justice and I do not always agree, but I wish to say without any reservation that hon. members greatly admired the patience and detail with which he dealt with these extremely important amendments to one of the heaviest and most important pieces of legislation of the House of Commons and the parliament of Canada. That work of course of necessity was bound to take a long time; but may I point out that the task of the Minister of Justice and of the committee would have been a hopeless one if the house had been suddenly confronted with that mass of legislation dealing with the rights of the individual in Canada under the Criminal Code. What made it possible for the minister to proceed in an orderly way, and what made it possible for the opposition to deal with it in an orderly way-and may I say that the chairman of the committee of our own party, the hon. member for Kamloops, is equally to be commended for the manner in which he followed section by section in the legislation before the house, as did other members of that committee-what made it possible for this legislation to be dealt with in an orderly way was that it was presented to the special committee early in the session. May I say that this could never have been done unless hon. members, and particularly the members of the legal committees of both sides of the house, had been able to examine this in advance, to check with legal experts outside, members of the bar association and others in regard to the implication of various amendments that were made.

Compare that, Mr. Chairman, with the act presented a short time ago to provide what is described as insurance for the civil servants. Here we had a bill which came before us without any opportunity being presented to hon. members to explore this subject, and without any opportunity for the representatives of the civil servants themselves really to present their case and check with their own members on what they thought of this unusual measure which had been brought forward by the Minister of Finance. There is a contrast, there is an illustration of the difference. There is proof of the advantage of having legislation come before us early.
However, during the course of any session new subjects of immense importance will arise, and naturally it will then be the responsibility of the government to deal with those subjects. However, when that is done, let us have the legislation just as quickly as we can and not at the last moment, as we have on some occasions during this session. I therefore urge the Prime Minister with all earnestness to see what can be done between now and the beginning of the next session to have the legislation which will interpret the decisions of the government drafted in advance and placed on the order paper. Then, when that is done, the moment that we can proceed with the completion of the debate on the speech from the throne, to have the committees set up and start work right away, and not months afterwards, as is usually the case. That would hasten the business of the session and not crowd those reports in at the last moment, as now happens. I repeat, there is only one person in this house who can successfully bring that about, and that is the Prime Minister, the man who, under our parliamentary system, has been entrusted with the immense power as well as responsibility of Prime Minister of Canada. With great earnestness I seek consideration of the views I have expressed.
The second point I mentioned was the judiciary. I need not for one moment seek to emphasize the importance of the judiciary to the Prime Minister, who is a great credit to the profession of which he is a highly honoured member. Both as past president and as honorary president of the Canadian Bar Association, he recognizes in all its significance the importance to Canada of an impartial judiciary. The only comment I propose to make in regard to this vitally important part of our constitutional organization in Canada is that, now appeals to the privy council have been abolished, the importance of every appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada is greater than ever before. I am sure every hon. member will agree with me that we have reason for great pride


in the history, the traditions and the personnel throughout the years of the Supreme Court of Canada. I would not wish to pass from this subject without saying that I know that all hon. members regret that time in its inevitable course has brought the resignation of the very distinguished Chief Justice who retired the day before yesterday, because there is not one of us whose admiration for his work in that high office is not in itself evidence of our satisfaction with what has been done in that court.
However, I simply seek to emphasize that in maintaining our great legal traditions, each appointment to the high court will of course become more important than ever before. Then, there are the courts of the provinces, the superior courts and the county courts. There it is of vital importance that the impartiality of each judge be an assurance of the extension of open-handed justice on every level. The record of our judiciary in this country on every level is one of which we have every reason to be proud. I make these comments only because we know that this subject is one that is under consideration, and to the distinguished member of the bar who occupies the office of Prime Minister I simply direct these remarks as an expression of hope on the part of every hon. member that the appointments that are made to the bench throughout Canada, whether it be the Supreme Court of Canada, the superior courts of the provinces or the county courts, will be appointments which will command the confidence and increasing respect of every Canadian.
The third subject that I propose to mention is the need of a conference between the federal and the provincial governments. It is not necessary, nor do I intend, to provoke some of the interjections that would doubtless be made if I sought to review at any length this extremely important subject.

As we near the end of this session I simply point out that it must be the responsibility of the Prime Minister, as chairman of the privy council, and it can be the responsibility of no one else, to call together between now and the time we meet again a conference of the federal and provincial governments to discuss the outstanding problems which are causing great concern to many Canadians.
I have no intention whatever of dealing with the merits of the issues which have been raised. No hon. member of this house, however, should disregard the fact that, unless there is some attempt to bring together the federal government and the governments of the provinces to explore the outstanding problems, increasing difficulties and friction may occur. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the subject under discussion in April was not a request to call a conference between now and the beginning of next session. The subject then under discussion related to facts that were then before the house. I would point out that the Prime Minister said this, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of June 1, 1954:
"Perhaps the most knotty problem of all which we had to face in recent years is that of the allocation of taxation revenues to enable governments in Canada at their different levels to carry out their constitutional responsibility.
"Under the terms of the British North America Act, both the provincial and federal authorities have the right to impose taxes in certain fields.
"Temporary agreements have been made with all the provinces but one, yet the basic problem of finding an acceptable solution that will allow all the provinces to preserve their rights and at the same time allow the governments to carry out their responsibilities, still remains."
It is to those words and that statement, and the problem before us now, Mr. Chairman, that I am directing my remarks, and I close my remarks in regard to this subject with the most earnest request to the Prime Minister that, whatever discussions may have taken place, whatever difference there may be, it be recognized that this is a subject of concern to all Canadians, that no one province alone is involved in this consideration, and that it would be extremely helpful to the parliament of Canada during the next session, in carrying out its responsibilities, if between now and that time a conference could be called at the instance of the Prime Minister, who is the only person who can call it, so that we know then something of what measure of agreement can be reached as to the procedure that will be followed in seeking a solution to our financial and constitutional problem.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I come to the fourth subject I mentioned, namely a commonwealth conference.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am discussing an item that relates to the position of the chairman of the privy council and it is only the chairman of the privy council who can, on behalf of Canada, take any steps that would effectively lead to a commonwealth conference. There is no other item of these estimates under which I could discuss this subject. I do so with the knowledge that next week the, shall I say, greatest parliamentary democrat in the world today is going to be a visitor here in Ottawa. I would strongly urge that at that time, when Sir Winston Churchill and Mr. Anthony Eden are here, the Prime Minister, as chairman of the privy council and Her Majesty the Queen's adviser, shall indicate, as an expression of the hope of the House of Commons and the people of Canada, that there be as soon as possible a conference of representatives of the nations of the commonwealth to consider those many things which may be of some advantage to all of us in the years ahead.
I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, to strain any ruling that might be given by suggesting in detail the subjects that would come forward. I would point out that when the leaders of the governments of the commonwealth met in London last year at the coronation the opportunity was limited for that kind of discussion which could lead to such beneficial results on an occasion such as this. Other conferences have taken place. Other conferences have failed. Only a few days ago the disarmament conference ended in complete failure. We know that the Geneva conference simply carries on with hope, and with little but hope. Here, however, is a conference of nations bound together in a common parliamentary system and with a common loyalty to the great traditions of the rule of law and the supremacy of parliament to which we all adhere. Here within this fellowship of nations are material and human resources which challenge the imagination of every one of us. Within this fellowship of member nations are more than 600 million people in Asia, in Europe, on the North American continent, and in the distant waters of the Pacific as well as on the great African continent. Here is something which offers hope to us and to all the rest of the world.
Let us take first things first. Here we have presented to us a chance to show what conferences can do and, out of the success of such a conference as this, to offer hope of greater success at other conferences in the
[The Chairman.]

years ahead. With respect to a wider friendship still with the United States our nearest neighbour, with France our ancient ally, and with the other nations with which we have been so closely associated, what greater challenge could we present than to show what we can do to our mutual advantage in marshalling the material as well as the human resources for the common benefit of ourselves and of all mankind? That is something that presents both a challenge and an opportunity to the Prime Minister, the chairman of the privy council, who in his recent trip around the world, saw something of the way in which Canada can and will be heard by other nations without any suggestion that we are trying to impose our will. Let no one fear that, in establishing more effective understanding within this great commonwealth-with all its tongues, all its races, all its creeds and all its traditions-we would in any way be creating any barriers between ourselves and the United States. On the contrary, we would offer to them greater evidence of how other conferences can proceed.
May I just quote a few words written in a magnificent editorial in the New York Times last Sunday when, in a great newspaper, an effort was made to dispose of the suggestion of the existence of deep and fundamental differences between the United States and the United Kingdom. May I quote these words:
There will be no deep conflict between this country and Britain: Not until Moscow adopts the golden rule as its sole policy, not until the moon turns blue-and not then.
Mr. Chairman, not until the moon turns blue-and not then-can there be misunderstanding between Canada and the United States. Let us give to them dramatic evidence of the fact that we are members of a wider world fellowship and that when they deal with us in a friendly manner, as they do, they deal with us as a partner in a wider association. That in itself would bring the great human and material resources of the United States still closer in harmony and in fellowship, with resulting immense benefits for us, for the commonwealth, for the United States and for the whole world.

In quite a number of cases property belonging to citizens of Ottawa was expropriated by the crown in 1947, and settlement has not yet been made. As the act now stands, it requires that settlement be made as at the time of expropriation, which in this case would be 1947. I am sure the Prime Minister will be the first to admit that if it is necessary for the state to take the property of citizens they should not be worse off because of the taking of the property than they would be if it had not been done.
I would suggest that the Exchequer Court Act be amended to make provision for settlement as at the time of expropriation or as at the time the state takes the property. I am sure the Prime Minister will agree that it would cost twice as much now in some cases to replace the property as it would have in 1947. I wish the Prime Minister would give consideration to introducing an amendment to this act next year so that settlement

may be made as at the time of expropriation or as at the time that payment is being made by the state.

I notice that the amount here is in excess of the sum of $300,000 provided for under the statute. It is over the $300,000 this year and it was also in excess of that last year. I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether it appears to be established as the result of experience that the amount provided by the statute is apparently inadequate, and that possibly the proper way to handle it might be to amend the statute to provide for a larger annual amount rather than having to go on voting supplementary amounts each year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Some consideration has been given to an amendment of the statute, but I think it is perhaps still desirable to have this distinction between the amount provided by the statute and the appropriation asked for each year. The amount provided by statute has been considered as the amount required to maintain the properties vested in the federal district commission, while under the other item we provide for the administration, care and upkeep of the grounds surrounding public buildings in Ottawa. Most of that work is done by the federal district commission so as not to have duplication of two organizations.
The federal district commission is responsible for the driveways and parkways, and has the equipment and personnel necessary for that work which is also appropriate to the kind of work that has to be done on the grounds surrounding government buildings. They have been required, therefore, over the last many years to have that personnel do the two jobs. The overhead is divided between the statutory grant and the vote on the basis of 50 per cent to each. The amount required for the proper maintenance of the grounds surrounding government buildings is increasing with the increase, of course, in the cost of labour, as well as the increase in the areas that have to be given attention. I feel it is really more economical than if public works had one organization and the federal district commission had another organization to take care of work of the same class. There is only one greenhouse which supplies all the bulbs and plants for landscaping both the parkways, driveways that are vested in the federal district commission and the other government property.

Then, this might be best
tidied up by providing in the statute itself that the federal district commission shall be
Supply-Privy Council responsible for the maintenance of the grounds, lawns, etc.; in other words, everything but the building itself.

When we get to the supplementary estimates the hon. gentleman will find a one dollar item to take care of that and regularize the procedure. In the meantime, the same thing has been done over the years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think I am out of order, but the general discussion we have had this morning on the administration of the privy council is one example of the many things that have prolonged this session. It is the first time in my experience that I have heard the suggestion the Prime Minister was responsible for everything that happened in Canada. It is the first time I have been described even as a democratic dictator. I have never felt that my dictatorship was of the same kind as is usually associated with that word.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Just so there will be no mistakes on the record, Mr. Chairman, if the record is examined it will be seen I did not apply that word to the Prime Minister. I said that textbooks used that term in relation to the power of the Prime Minister under our parliamentary system.

With respect to the four points mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition, I believe everyone is agreed that we did make a genuine effort this time to have most of the legislation on the order paper within the first week that parliament was sitting. As early as November 18, parliament having met on November 12, there were 6 bills and 7 resolutions on the order paper; by December 8, there were
11	bills and 5 resolutions; on January 19,
12	bills and 4 resolutions; and by February
10, 14 bills and 3 resolutions. But I confess I have been disappointed at the time it took to get the drafts of some of the subsequent bills that had to be brought before parliament.	I can assure the Leader of the
Opposition and the house that I was just as disappointed as anyone else over the fact that it did take some time, but I assure the house also there is a serious effort to have legislation on the order paper as early as possible.
With respect to the judiciary, I think the Leader of the Opposition and all members of parliament are in agreement that we are

Supply-Privy Council very fortunate in having had gentlemen of the character we have had in the administration of justice. As a very old personal friend of the Chief Justice, who retired at midnight between June 21 and June 22 from his responsibilities, I wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition for the very kind remarks he has made about him. I know that the hon. gentleman has achieved what could be the highest ambition of any young man who enters into the profession of law, and who advances progressively and rapidly in that career. He was a distinguished barrister: that I know from having crossed swords with him almost half a century ago. He was also a distinguished superior court judge of the superior court of Quebec: that I know from having been before him on more than one occasion in that capacity. He was a distinguished puisne judge of the supreme court, and subsequently a distinguished Chief Justice of that court.
It was not my privilege to appear before him while he was Chief Justice because events had caused me to follow other paths. But I had been before him on many occasions when he was one of the puisne judges of the court. I know that it will be a great satisfaction to him to have had this tribute to his career expressed in this house. I do wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition for making it possible to have that tribute expressed this morning.
The hon. member suggests that there should be a dominion-provincial conference. There certainly will be a dominion-provincial conference just as soon as we can have something concrete to discuss in that conference. With respect to the fiscal relations, they are governed by a contract, in so far as nine of the provinces are concerned, which neither the Leader of the Opposition nor I would wish to repudiate. They have been contracts made in good faith by those provinces and so far as we are concerned they must be carried out in the spirit in which they were made. There would have to be some alternative suggested. In discharging the responsibilities, which are not of the over-all extent mentioned by the hon. member for Lethbridge but which are nevertheless heavy, I would not wish to call a conference and say to them: "Well now, gentlemen, you are here and what are we going to talk about; what can we suggest or consider as an alternative to what we have?"
That is one reason why serious consideration should be given, and is being given, to the suggestion from the successor of the Leader of the Opposition, as premier of


Ontario, of a preliminary discussion at the level of high, technical officials. With respect to a commonwealth conference-
Is that the economic committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The economic committee that has been referred to, that was referred to in 1945.
We are all, I think, in both the federal and the provincial fields, anxious to find something that will be satisfactory; because we are all not only Canadians but, I think, good Canadians. And we are all living together, and are bound to continue to live together. It is unfortunate that so much is required for public services at all levels; and it is particularly unfortunate that the federal authorities have to take such a large part of the taxation that is available for the services. That creates a difficult situation. I will not go beyond that.
With respect to a commonwealth conference, there is no doubt that that is something that will arise in the course of the informal conversations we will be having. But from the impressions I brought back from the East, a conference to deal with matters affecting the East would, I think, have a better chance of being successful if it were one that was sought by the governments of the East, and that implied no possible suggestion that we of the West wanted to direct the proper policies for the solution of these eastern difficulties.
There has been a suggestion that there be a conference either of prime ministers or of ministers of foreign affairs; and I think the suggestion has been made that it would be preferable if that conference were promoted by the governments of the East rather than by the governments of the West. In any event the aim would be, as the Leader of the Opposition said, something that would be helpful. And it will be through informal discussions that we will find out what is apt to be most helpful.
Then, with respect to the questions of the hon. member for Lethbridge, I must confess that I get no confidential information from any communist sources, and that I am not cognizant of what may be the real line of the communists for North America in 1954. The hon. member certainly was not putting his first question as anything more than just a preliminary, when he asked, "Do we want to win the cold war? Does the Prime Minister want to win the cold war?" The Prime Minister does not feel that he can win the cold war; the Prime Minister feels that Canada, and all the free countries, are doing their best and will continue to do their best to

win the cold war; because together they wish and they hope to win the cold war.
I do not think X would be prepared to suggest establishing as a proper precedent a procedure on estimates under which we would not consider the amounts to be voted, but simply use the discussion of the estimates as an opportunity to discuss anything with which a minister whose estimates are under consideration may be concerned. I think it may develop that there is much to be said for the suggestion that the details, respecting some departments, might perhaps be considered more appropriately in working committees, and that when they then come back to the house it might be proper to have these discussions on very interesting but somewhat academic aspects of government policy. But it would be difficult to have the business of the house arranged in such a way when there would not be several occasions when somewhat different aspects of the same questions would be up for discussion.
I do not think any of us believe it is by rigid rules that matters of that kind can be dealt with. It does not matter very much what the language of a rule may be; if there is a serious attempt to go around it, my experience in the house has been that that attempt is usually successful. So he will try not to give the opposition parties any occasion for feeling that anything is being held back, or any reason for feeling that we are not doing our best to make it possible to have the business of the country discussed in an orderly and perhaps in a somewhat more expeditious way than has been the case during this session.
But in order to proceed more expeditiously each one of us will have to be doing his best to that end. We will continue to try to have the legislation brought down just as early as possible, because we agree that that will be helpful.
I apologize to you, Mr. Chairman, for having taken this time; but I thought that, these general remarks having been made, it might have been looked upon by my hon. friends opposite as somewhat discourteous if I did not make some attempt to reply. And it is for that reason that I did venture to make these few comments.

Mr. Chairman, this is the item covering the general administration-estimates of the Clerk, and I would like to know what the situation is now with regard to the terms of employment of the protective staff of the House of Commons. We have here I think the finest corps-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but I might inform him that that subject comes under the estimates of the Sergeant-at-Arms.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say just a brief word under this item. First of all, I wonder if I could have the privilege of welcoming back to the floor of the house for a few moments our esteemed first commoner. Along with that welcome I should like to express once again my words of appreciation and commendation both to His Honour, Mr. Speaker, and to his deputy minister-I believe that is the status that is occupied by the Clerk of this house-for the excellent way in which they are administering the affairs of the House of Commons in so far as they come under their direction.
The one question I would like to put to Mr. Speaker relates to the pension situation in so far as the employees of the House of Commons are concerned. I know His Honour will recall that some years ago some of us had quite a bit to say about the desirability of having a pension plan for House of Commons employees, particularly those not otherwise covered. In the main the need for a special plan such as that which we used to advocate has been obviated by the change from the Civil Service Superannuation Act to the Public Service Superannuation Act. As I understand it the main difference between the two is that the act we now have goes beyond civil servants and includes all those employed in the public service providing they meet the conditions laid down in the Public Service Superannuation Act.
I have in my hand a very interesting little booklet prepared by the public service superannuation branch of the Department of Finance at Ottawa entitled "Your Superannuation Plan", on page 7 of which I read these words:
With a few exceptions, this act provides that every full time employee in the public service, male or female, married or single, with an annual
[The Chairman.]
rate of salary of $900 or more, will start to build up his superannuation credits after no more than a year of substantially continuous employment.
I realize that under that provision any employee of the House of Commons who is here the year round, whether that employee is on a permanent or classified basis or not, is covered by the new Public Service Superannuation Act providing his or her salary is $900 or more per annum. But what about our sessional employees? I am thinking of all the people who work here for as much of the year as we require them and who may earn more than $900 for that portion of the year and come back from year to year. Are they covered? If not, is consideration being given to finding some way in which they can be covered?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The sessional employees are not covered but it is our understanding that some consideration is being given to the establishment of some scheme or pension plan which would apply to sessional employees in the public service. As the hon. member knows, we have several employees who are hired on a sessional basis and cannot be employed otherwise because of the nature of the business which the House of Commons carries on. The house is in session only for so many months each year and therefore once the session is over we have to sever our connections with many of these employees.
Our difficulty at the moment is that once they have been in our service for 25 sessions, or 10, 15, or 20 years, we feel there should be some way of retiring them with certain compensation. As it is now, they are retired with, I believe, one month's leave together with one month's pay for every five years they have been in the service. I must point out in that connection that up until recently the system was that employees who had been working on a sessional basis or who had been working here all the year round and who were not under the Civil Service Act were upon retirement receiving only $100 together with $10 for every year of service. Take now, for example, a man who had been working here for 10 years. When he retired all he received was $100 and $10 for every year, which would mean $200 for his 10 years' service, and that would have been the end of the matter.
This situation was carefully considered and it was felt that pending any other arrangements the employees who had to be retired should be given the same benefits as those which they could enjoy if placed under the civil service commission, namely one month's retirement leave plus one month's pay for every five years' service. In other words,

an employee who had been working here 10 years would receive three months' full pay. That puts them in a position which is perhaps six or seven times better than the position in which they were a few months ago.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 am glad that an improvement has been made along the lines that have been indicated with respect to employees who retire, and I welcome even more Mr. Speaker's assurance that the matter of some pension arrangement for employees in this group is under consideration. From the very good attention which the Speaker and the Clerk give to all these matters that come under their jurisdiction I know that, if they are pursuing it, it will be pursued with diligence. They certainly have my backing and, I believe, that of hon. members generally.
I just want to say this further word. I want to express the hope that as little time as possible will be lost in bringing this matter to a conclusion, for this reason amongst others. So often it happens that after a time employees who have been in a service for a certain number of years are accorded certain pension rights and with those rights is accorded the privilege of going back and covering past service. When that time comes, frequently the amount of money involved in covering past service can be quite a huge sum and it can become quite a problem for some of these people to know whether or not to try to cover that past service. For that reason I hope there will be as little delay as possible in dealing with the matter of some definite pension arrangement for all our House of Commons employees who come back year after year even although they may be on a sessional basis. I am sure I can speak for hon. members generally when I say to the Speaker and to the Clerk that, in their pursuit of this matter, they have our support.

I should like to say a word in support of what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, and to commend Mr. Speaker for the action that has already been taken. He is well aware of the fact that there are in the House of Commons members who have already interested themselves in this problem and who are prepared to support any move that may be made along that line. The sessional employees have given and are giving faithful service. Through perhaps an oversight in the years gone by, the question of superannuation for them has not been considered. It is a welcome move now. We hope that the Speaker will be encouraged by the support
Supply-Legislation
he is getting from members of the committee and that he will press on with this particular needed reform.

I just want to say that I heartily support the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I had intended to make similar comments in two or three minutes but he has taken the wind out of my sails. I shall therefore get on his boat.

There is one point I should like to bring out. It has reference to the comparative amounts spent for help required by the office of the Leader of the Opposition and by the leaders of other groups. In the details given with regard to the office of the Leader of the Opposition I notice that there are seven on that particular staff, which is composed of a private secretary, a secretary, a clerk and four stenographers. Mr. Chairman, I would not want that number of helpers on that staff to be reduced. In fact, if the Leader of the Opposition finds that he needs even more help, I would be quite willing to say that he should have it. However, there is this point to be considered. We know that the Leader of the Opposition occupies a rather special place on the opposition benches in the House of Commons. He is recognized as the leader of the official opposition. Nevertheless, the opposition or the work of his party has no reason, particularly, to be any more effective than that of the other smaller groups. The point I want to put over to you, Mr. Chairman, is that, when it comes to the matter of performing a vital function as leaders of opposition groups, the other leaders have just as much work to do as has the Leader of the Opposition. Yet the leaders of the other groups have to be satisfied with one or two on their staff.
I am therefore putting up this plea. It seems to me that more help should be given to the leaders of the other parties in respect of secretarial help, research and that sort of thing. I know that the leader of this party is exceptionally busy. Frankly, I do not know how he is able to get through all his work and do the job he is really doing here in the House of Commons. As I say, I have no idea whatsoever of intimating that seven on the staff in the office of the Leader of the Opposition are too many. I would not say so. However, I say that the help and the staff given to the leaders of the other groups should be increased.

203. Estimates of the Sergeant-at-Arms, $726,540.

May we have an explanation of the conditions of service of the protective

Supply-Legislation
force of the House of Commons? I have in mind particularly whether they are on a five-day week, the number of hours they work each day, and also what provisions are made for their holidays. I believe that the conditions are not nearly as favourable as they are in the civil service generally and in industry. I would ask His Honour to outline just what these conditions are and what prospects there are for improvement.
From my observations-and I think every hon. member of the committee will agree- this protective force of ours is doing a splendid job. I do not believe there is a finer force in the country. They not only have to keep order around the building but, in addition, they come in contact with hundreds of thousands of tourists every year. I do not know what is the number of tourists who go through this House of Commons in the course of a year, but I believe it runs into several hundred thousand. It is not always an easy job to handle, in a friendly and kindly way, these groups going through the building. Yet I have never known any other type of contact throughout the years I have been here. I think it is really wonderful the way these men handle the people who are in and out of the building. They of all people should have up-to-date working conditions. Perhaps His Honour could explain to us just what the conditions are at the present time?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I agree with everything the hon. member has said with regard to the loyalty and the effectiveness of the services rendered by the members of the protective staff. The problem presented to them during a few months of the year is the additional work due to the number of welcomed tourists who come to Ottawa. This was a matter of concern to the Clerk and to myself, and we have examined the situation. Of course, in years gone by we did not have as many tourists visiting us as we now have. There are members of the protective staff who, for one reason or another, do not act as guides. There are several of them who have to perform these additional duties, and who have to take around the building these groups of students and visitors and explain to them what is to be seen around the buildings. That caused them to work during the summer months on a more active basis than those who were only doing ordinary shift work. Having that in mind, we wanted to give some adequate remuneration in order to cover this additional work. That was a very difficult problem to settle because we did not want to put one constable in a position that would be unfair compared with the position of another. It was decided that many of the corporals who do this work of guiding

tourists around the building would be promoted to the rank of sergeant and would receive the additional amount of pay that that would necessarily involve. I think this went through the house recently after recommendation by the civil service commission, and if they are not now in receipt of the additional money which this promotion commands they should be receiving it very shortly.
There was another feature involved in the general promotion of corporals to the rank of sergeant. Arrangements had to be made to make sure that there would be a sergeant in charge of every shift throughout the week in order to bring about a fair distribution of the number of hours they have to work in a week. This building has to be protected every day of the week, including holidays. As far as the holidays of these men are concerned, I am not quite sure as to the exact position. The Clerk has given me certain information but I am not quite sure that I recall every detail. Perhaps I might give the correct explanation to the hon. member privately if that is agreeable to him.
However, I am certain of one thing. From conversations I have had with the chief of the protective staff and with the Sergeant-at-Arms, under whose jurisdiction the protective staffs happens to fall, I can say that there are no complaints whatsoever as to the conditions under which these men work at the moment, either with respect to hours of work or the holiday period.

If I were His Honour I would not be too sure of that. I think he should make a thorough investigation to find out what the conditions are. For example, do these men get their holidays all at one time or are they given a certain length of time at one period and then further time later? I understand there is some such arrangement, and I do not see why they should not be given a proper holiday all at one time in the same way as other civil servants. I should also like to know whether or not they are on a five-day week and how long they work each day. The house has been sitting much longer than usual this session and probably will in future sessions. The time has come to review the whole situation. It may be that a larger staff is necessary. Can His Honour tell us something further about holidays, the length of the work week and the number of hours worked in a day?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I agree with the hon. member that something will have to be done by way of establishing better conditions with respect to the number of hours these gentlemen have to work, but that is under consideration at the moment. The first move in this respect

was taken by eliminating the rank of corporal and promoting the corporals to the status of sergeants, thus giving the chief of the protective staff more officers to take care of the direction of the men throughout the week.
One must keep in mind that the tourist season extends from the first of May until the first of November, and it is very difficult to arrange for the men of the protective staff to take their holidays during the summer months when most of them are employed guiding the thousands and thousands of tourists who visit the capital during those months. They are entitled to one month's holiday. With respect to holidays during the year to which they are entitled and which they are not able to take, their annual holiday is lengthened by the number of days on which they were called upon to work when they really should not have been on the job. I am talking about statutory holidays and the like.
As to the number of hours worked in a week, there are three shifts of eight hours each. However, as I said, we are looking into that situation. After all, it is not very long ago that the five-day 40-hour week was established and certain readjustment is necessary. But the difficulty is increased in the case of the protective staff because of the fact that while certain members of the force who have been here for many years do very well the ordinary work of the protective staff they do not work as guides during the tourist season. That creates difficulties in the establishment of an over-all uniform system for all the men because while they are all qualified as protective staff employees they may not all be particularly qualified for the position of guide which is an important duty that many of them have to perform in addition to their ordinary duties as members of the protective staff.
I can assure the hon. member that the point he has raised is receiving careful consideration at the moment, and we hope to be in a position to put these men on a basis which will give them full satisfaction and will be fair to all of them. So far as conditions of employment and personnel are concerned, from the contacts and conversations I have had with the gentleman referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as my deputy minister, I can say that no one is more human in his approach to these various employment problems, and I am satisfied that, having studied the matter as he has in the last few months, he will soon come forward with a recommendation that will be acceptable to hon. members.

Apparently the force is not yet on the 40-hour week?
Supp ly-Legis lation

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not quite, but they will be. We are gradually working toward that under the new system, and the first step was taken by abolishing the position of corporal in order to create more sergeants. We are on our way to establishing something which will amount to the 40-hour week.

I shall only detain the committee for a minute or two because I presume that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is expecting a lengthy debate on his estimates. I want to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and to express my personal appreciation of the efficiency and courtesy of the protective staff, the messenger staff, the elevator staff and the other staffs of the House of Commons. They work under somewhat unusual and trying conditions at times involving on occasion long hours, and I think all members appreciate the work they do.
I also want to express my appreciation to Mr. Speaker and his deputy for their readiness to give sympathetic consideration to any staff problem that is brought to their attention. Their sense of justice and their willingness to remedy anything that appears to be wrong is in our best traditions.

Before the item carries, I should like to bring something to the attention of the Speaker. I am not sure it has to do with his estimates, but I am sure he will bring it to the attention of the proper person. I have never seen any member of the cabinet or the Speaker visiting the peace tower, but I suggest that there are thousands and thousands of visitors who do. It would be most helpful, and a service the parliament buildings should provide, if around the peace tower, on all four sides, bronze plaques were laid on top of the ramparts so that a person could look at the plaque and easily ascertain the important historical sites and buildings around the city of Ottawa. This sort of thing is done in many monuments, and if you happen to have visited Washington monument in the District of Columbia, you will find they have very beautiful ones there, which are very helpful.
I am sure that if the members of the government had heard many of the remarks of visitors in the peace tower, they would have realized that some type of map laid on top of the ramparts of the peace tower would be of great advantage.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the words of the hon. member will reach the Department of Public Works and most careful consideration will be given to his thought.

I do not like to rise to bring up trivial matters, especially at this late hour,

Supply-Finance
but I should like to draw the attention ol hon. members to one particular point. I am wondering whether or not there is close enough liaison between those who are responsible for what takes place on the lawns outside in front of the parliament buildings and the protective staff here. Very often there are festivities taking place out there, usually on a Sunday afternoon, and when you make inquiries no one seems to know what is going on. I have had that experience two or three times. Sometimes there are activities there that are very enjoyable and inspiring. I recall that two or three Sundays ago there was a parade of cadets, and it was inspiring indeed. I have yet to get any information concerning what was going on; nobody seems to know very much about it.
There is just one other matter, and that is the old problem of parking space. I know that we do not want to have the grounds marred in any way, and I would not like to see a lot of cars lined up in front of the buildings, blocking the view. I know that is a problem that the Sergeant-at-Arms has had to wrestle with, and I am going to make this suggestion. I do not suppose it is new to him. I am wondering what purpose the lawn on the west side of the west block serves. I doubt very much whether anyone goes out there very often. Could that not be paved and turned into a parking lot? I do not think it would spoil the appearance of the building at all. It is too far removed and is up on top of a hill. Very few people pass that way, and I think the area would accommodate quite a number of cars. I make these two suggestions, and it is not necessary for Mr. Speaker to reply to them. Perhaps he could take them under advisement.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.
