speechtext: 104. Departmental administration, $1,843,627.
Is the minister going to make any remarks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman; I usually make my remarks in the course of the budget speech and on a variety of other occasions during the year. I am ready to answer questions, but I have never felt any useful purpose was served by my making any extended statement on my estimates.
The minister was very generous in not adding that he could not see there was any useful purpose in anyone else making any extended remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I welcome that.

The minister is much too polite to say anything like that. However, I hope I can show my appreciation and the reputation I hope I have earned for brevity by not taking more than a few minutes. The actual finance estimates in themselves invite very little comment, because, of the $936 million which is to be voted, only $34 million is really to be voted and the rest is provided by statute. A great deal of the money to be provided is for interest on government debts, grants to provinces, and so on. There are indeed only one or two items to which I want to refer particularly.
One to which I want to refer particularly was mentioned by the Auditor General in his report, at page 33, and it has to do with advances to the old age security fund. Hon. members will recall that the fund is operated under a special act. There are three taxes earmarked for it, and for reasons which seemed inadequate to many people in this house it has been dealt with separately and has involved a special accounting problem of its own to which the Auditor General refers. There has been a deficiency, and it has had to be dealt with. The minister referred to it himself at pages 3729 and 3730 of Hansard for April 6, 1954. I wish to refer to it very briefly.
In the year 1952-53 there was a deficiency of some $99 million, which was taken care of by an advance from the consolidated revenue fund. The minister, having carried that as an asset, and that is the reason really underlying the Auditor General's comment, has now written it off out of reserves which have been built up since 1940 or 1941 and Which now amount to something like $500 million or $600 million. This reserve is a genuine reserve because it has been taken year by year out of the annual receipts. The only reason I am referring to this, and I presume the only reason the Auditor General raised it, is perhaps to remind us again of the curious complicated situation which has arisen by reason of this special compartment in which we have kept the old age security fund. Perhaps the minister will later say a word as to whether he thinks that fund is coming to be anywhere near self-sustaining.
I am going to say very little about expenditures. A great deal has been said about them. Expenditures get to be like the weather, I am afraid. We talk about them, but do little or nothing. Gradually and unconsciously, and perhaps foolishly, we have slipped into a position where we apparently feel that we can afford to spend nearly $5 billion, without saying very much about

it. It seems almost the other day the minister was telling us, just before the Korea episode, that he did not believe we could expect to spend much less than we were spending that year, which was $2,400 million; in other words, about half of what we are spending now. The minister said to us then that we could not spend less than that if we wanted to get the things that we were getting at the time. It was hard to argue against that- that if we wanted those things, then we had to pay for them. Our economy is operating now at a substantially higher level, of course, and those who are good at figures will no doubt tell us that we can stand a lot more than we could stand then. Actually, we are standing it, and, in a way, we are becoming rather complacent about it.
I have quoted before, and I shall quote again, what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said last February about the budget. He said it was decided that this would be a year to loosen the purse strings and step up our public works program. It is hard to expect, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce, presumably with the approval of his colleagues, makes a remark of that kind, that economy is going to be in the air. And it is not going to be in the air until people become economy minded.
At the present time it seems impossible to interest them in doing very much along that line. Nevertheless I wish to register a question about this complacent attitude. Sometimes we are not as rich as we think we are. Sometimes people who have been riding along easily and making heavy expenditures find that they would have been wiser not to do so. Indeed, there are signs now that we are coming to the proof of the pudding. We have been prospering largely by reason of huge expenditures. Certainly we have a huge productive capacity. As I go around the outskirts of the city in which I live, and see the enormous expansion taking place, sometimes I become almost alarmed -although I entirely deny the title of pessimist.
I ask myself this question: Are we sure we are going to be able to sell all these goods? I remind myself, and I also remind the committee, that one of the reasons which enter largely into our prosperity at the moment is that the government is spending a lot of money. In other words we, the taxpayers, are providing a lot of money-billions of dollars of it-which go into expenditures, and which produce the same kind of wages as any other investment. We roll along, and this money accumulates, and everything seems just grand.
Supply-Finance
But while we are doing that, and while the minister very appropriately points out the large amounts of public expenditure going into the gross national product, I point out that one aspect of these expenditures is that they are entering into our costs and increasing our costs, and if we are reaching the stage of really stiff competition, as many people believe we are, it is going to be a very important question to face.
Meanwhile I am not going to say any more about the problem of economy. We are not going to grapple with economy until there is a feeling for it abroad. That is the essence of democracy. You will hardly get a government to go very much ahead of public opinion. If the government can spend money, as they have been spending it, and go back and get elected, they just say, "So what!" They say, "Why should we not go on? The people like expenditures." And I think a good many people do. Economy comes only when we reach the stage of saying, "Can we do without it?" So long as we keep on saying, "It is very pleasant and convenient to have it"-which we have been saying-we will not get anywhere in curbing expenditures.
I know the minister feels that he is actually a kind of ogre to the other departments, that he treats them very rough, and that if it were not for him expenditures would be twice as great. And that may all be true. But I am reiterating what I have said before, that we will never get anywhere in economies until people are told, "That is what is to be spent, and no more".
As I said a moment ago, the estimates of the Department of Finance, so far as their details are concerned, do not invite much by way of comment. But the finance department has a significance which goes far beyond these actual items that we are voting this afternoon.
The tentacles of the finance department reach everywhere. Nobody can escape the long arm of the tax collector. The minister fully recognizes that in his budget speech. In fact the budget speech is really what is known in the United States as a speech on the state of the nation. That is one of the things which give the budget speech the importance that it has. In other words, we all recognize-and I am sure the minister recognizes it first of all-that tax measures cannot be considered in a vacuum.
The minister's speech covered as I said the whole state of the nation. We may think that it is always optimistic. This year I think the minister's glasses were a little bit rose-coloured and the speech had the aspects of a lullaby. But people like lullabies.

Supply-Finance
I am accused of being a pessimist, but I deny that. To those who would accuse me I would reply that I think the ministers seem to me to indulge in orgies of optimism, whereas I am only a moderate drinker. And we reach somewhat different results.
We have grown somewhat accustomed to living in a boom in Canada. It has become embodied in our thinking. And now, if we have reached a stage where there is even a levelling off, it will give us quite a shock. In other words we have to run fast to keep where we are. If there is even a flattening out it will seem like being on the skids.
The minister reviewed 1953, and declared the gross national product as satisfactory. Of course 1953 constituted a record. I should like to read very briefly one or two of the statements the minister made in commenting on 1954. As reported at page 3727 he said:
It is clear that industry as a whole has such confidence in the future of the economy that it intends to undertake greater capital investment than ever before.
I think that is correct. Then he goes on to say:
The expenditures of the federal government on goods and services, as well as those of provincial and municipal governments, will increase moderately this year.
And finally, on the same page:
My general conclusion is that our national product in 1954 will be at least equal to 1953, and probably higher: in other words I think that an upswing in the second half of the year will more than compensate for the declines that are evident in certain branches of industry at present.
Now, as I say, we should remember that 1953 was a record year; and we should not be entirely disappointed if 1954 does not quite keep up. I think there are a great many signs that 1954 is not going to keep up to the 1953 level, and that we should prepare ourselves accordingly.
I want to add to what I said about the effect of government expenditures on cost. Because if we are getting into a more and more competitive field, then I think we have to remind ourselves of the portion of our selling cost which comes from taxes. I am thinking of the condition at home and abroad, but particularly abroad. Of course, at home both the sales tax and the income tax affect prices. Abroad the sales tax does not affect prices of our exports.
But, to return to the income tax, let me point out that a very considerable portion of the income tax on corporations, which yielded last year some $1,200 million, is and must be reflected in costs. The personal income tax, to the extent that it results in increased wages, is also reflected in costs.

I think we have to face the fact-and a very unpleasant fact it is-that the expectation we all had that when income tax would be spread out widely, that would make people economy minded, has not proved to be so. The income tax has in fact come to be regarded as just another deduction from pay envelopes. I think it is no exaggeration to say there is a feeling that there is almost a right, at any rate, a very strong argument, to get an increase in pay to compensate for any increase in the income tax. That is a matter which again will be significant if we are entering into a situation where we are going to face a real test of earning on these many billions of dollars of expenditures in a competitive market. The question of taxation will strike us from an angle that we have perhaps been rather insensitive to in these last years.
In his budget speech the minister did not neglect this. He told us of the difficulties that were arising. He mentioned tariff applications. I want to read two paragraphs from a recent letter of the minister. The letter is dated May 12 and is addressed to the tariff board. In this letter he directs them to conduct an inquiry into wool. The letter reads in part as follows:
I have received numerous representations from the woollen industry in Canada to the effect that, as a result of price changes, the 50-cent maximum duty prescribed under the British preferential rate of tariff item 554b has become anomalous and unrealistic, and that, as a consequence, the industry has suffered, and is suffering, serious injury; indeed, it has been claimed that the continued existence of the industry is in jeopardy.
Undoubtedly the Canadian government will wish to give special consideration to this tariff item, and particularly to the specific maximum thereunder, in the coming GATT renegotiations, and therefore will wish to have readily available all relevant information concerning the Canadian woollen industry and concerning as well the implications for the Canadian economy of imports of wool fabrics from the United Kingdom.
I am quite satisfied the minister wrote that letter with great unwillingness.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, on the contrary; I was very anxious to write it.

Let me explain myself. I am quite satisfied the minister regretted the situation which had arisen to cause the writing of the letter. Let me put it that way. I perhaps should warn the minister that he will be regarded with dark suspicion by the Winnipeg Free Press for even indulging in this inquiry, but I have no doubt he will be able to satisfy them that anything-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister believes in getting the facts, as my hon. friend knows.

I am telling the minister that it may be of use to suggest that anything that he does that the Free Press does not like has been suggested to him by the naughty Tories. They will accept that explanation very readily indeed.
The minister-and this is the last reference I want to make to his prediction in the speeches-refers to the United States and to the upswing which he hopes and expects is going to come there in the last six months of the year. It seems to me that what can be fairly said of the present business situation is this. No serious person doubts the continued forward movement of Canada over the years. Nothing can prevent the development of our great resources, and the prosperity which that will bring, but nevertheless there may be minor hollows and rises in the general course. I think it is perfectly clear that since last autumn business activity has had a gentle tapering off; however I do not think anyone has the right to say there is any sign of a sharp drop. But we are at the moment in a way on the defensive, and the dynamic factors which have sped us along with almost breathless speed are, for the moment, definitely weaker. One of the questions that arise in men's minds is whether in this period of boom expansion we have built and expanded almost regardless of cost. I heard only yesterday of factories built where the costs had been vastly in excess of the estimate. That is not a new story, of course, but the person who told me this- and he was a shrewd observer-said, I sometimes wonder whether we have really had enough regard to costs. I heard the other day of one factory making the expenditure of a good many millions which is approaching completion where they were evidently perturbed. They are within a couple of months of production, but they have no business at the moment. That is one of those things that may cure itself.
It has become fashionable in certain quarters to suggest that anyone who is not going through the motions of a cheer-leader is dragging down the economy. My feeling is- and I hope we shall get something today-we are entitled to get from the government their serious assessment of the situation as it is today. It is almost three months since the minister spoke to us. He gave us his serious assessment then. We are going off now for months, and I hope he will bring us up to date today. What we want from the government is realism. We want to be treated as adults, and allowed to see the situation as it appears to the government, because sermons and admonitions are not enough. There are various classes and groups of people at the
Supply-Finance
present time who are not finding it too easy and who are facing a competition such as they have not faced for some time, and of course the more competitive the situation the more serious the condition.
In a recent article of the Wall Street Journal there was a letter from the staff reporter which causes one a good deal of thought. This reporter had been here. He was reporting on the large import into Canada of United States goods, and said this:
Moreover, the larger-seale mass production techniques of many American producers permit them to offer many of their goods at prices well below those of Canadian manufacturers whose operations are geared to smaller and therefore higher-cost output.
Then he gives this illustration, which troubles one because it brings up very vividly the position of a Canadian manufacturer. He says this:
And look at what Empire Brass Manufacturing Company Limited has been doing. This firm, one of Canada's biggest plumbing fixture makers, in recent weeks has actually imported some United States made faucets and similar hardware and supplied them to its customers in place of its own Empire brand items. Meanwhile 800 workers at Empire's own London, Ontario, factory have been reduced to a four-day work week.
That, Mr. Chairman, just brings back to our minds the fact that for fifteen years we have been in a seller's market. Now, apparently we are in a buyer's market. The implications and results of that are definite, and could become very serious.
As to exports abroad, I am going to say nothing. We have had the classic question of wheat debated here, and I am not going to do more that remind people that it is a kind of symbol of what other exporters are going to find as well. I have referred to the optimism of the ministers. That is good; nobody wants anything else, but I want to mention in passing that some groups in Canada may be disposed to query this optimism. I refer to the textile people, and I need not do more than mention the letter which the minister has written. Then there are the electrical appliance people. I have already referred to Empire Brass. Farm income is down from $2,154 million after expansion and depreciation in 1951 to $1,900 million in 1952 and $1,656 million in 1953. These are the latest figures I could get. Business failures are troublesome. In the first quarter of 1954 they jumped to 680 compared with 382 last year, and liabilities jumped to $17,660,000 as against $7,151,000. These are serious things.
I come to the question of the maritimes, and I want to mention only what was said yesterday about the failure to decentralize. I

Supply-Finance
think that is a place where we can legitimately complain against the government because I think there have been neglected opportunities with regard to the position of the maritimes. When we consider the amounts we spent, first of all during the war, and even more important perhaps, since the war, I can see no reason why more could not have been done. I have in mind the answers given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If we had a real sense of solidarity here and a feeling that our country cannot be prosperous if a substantial section is unprosperous, then I think a more co-operative attitude might have been taken with regard to the maritimes. There is trouble in the retail trade and I shall do nothing more than refer to a speech made by Mr. Burton of Simpsons-Sears the other day in which he, himself a huge retailer, referred, with sympathy and understanding and I am sure sincerity, to the position of the smaller retailers and, incidentally, remarked on the injuries which they were suffering by that ill-omened piece of legislation, the Resale Price Maintenance Act of two years ago.
Now, we come to the United States tariff attitude and I quote from a statement made in Montreal the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as reported in the Montreal Gazette for June 17:
There is an obvious surge in the world today towards freer trade, Bight Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce, said here last night.
And he told 150 commonwealth business leaders that their countries had made "great progress in getting rid of import controls which were rendered necessary by the post-war emergency."
If one considers the over-all situation it seems to me the minister had the wrong word because we cannot talk about this situation without including the United States; and to say there is any "surge" in the United States today towards freer trade is just a misuse of words. I am afraid that if we were accurate we would say that the tide is ebbing and not flowing. At the present time there is an anxiously awaited report from the federal tariff commission, I think it is called, in which it is greatly feared that zinc, lead, and fillets may be affected, which, added to the other things already affected, would certainly not be a good thing for our exporters.
Again, Mr. Chairman, one cannot ask the government for unreasonable things, but one can, I think, ask them for direct answers to direct questions, and I suggest we are not getting them. The situation reminds me a little of the exercises in our French textbooks at school, which I have mentioned before in this house which were in the form of question and answer and often the answer had nothing to do with the question. For
[Mr. Macdonnell.l
example, the question would be, "Have you the pen of the teacher?" and the answer would be, "No, but I have the knife of the butcher." In the same way, when we ask the Minister of Finance questions, imagine for example when a manufacturer comes to him and asks him if he can do anything to help him cut down costs, or do anything about taxes, the minister would reply, "No, but you remember me speaking about sharpening pencils, curtailing the cost of management, and making labour more efficient." In addition, if I may paraphrase the answer which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given to those who asked, have you sold the 1953 crop, his answer might be, "No, but we had 32 [DOT] 5 per cent of the world wheat trade during 1951-52."
Now, Mr. Chairman, no doubt you and the minister will be glad to know that I am almost finished, and again I might urge that what we are asking of the government is quite reasonable and that I hope the minister will make a statement today. We want the problem stated. Of course, our future is bright in the main but there are special problems at the moment and I would like to hear the government's assessment of these problems. I think we are entitled to ask the government to give us a much better performance than has been the case in the maritimes. I think their efforts at decentralization have been weak and ineffective in the extreme. If in past history there had not been much broader and more courageous views than those adopted by the government at this moment, we would not be where we are today.
Another thing I want to mention is the purchases from Britain, mentioned yesterday by the hon. member for Eglinton, and I want to reiterate what he said then about the remark of Mr. Duncan of the Massey-Harris Company, who advanced the view that by switching seven per cent of the United States purchases to the United Kingdom we could balance our trade with the United Kingdom. That, of course, brings in the whole question of defence purchases from the United Kingdom which seem to me to be far below what they might be.
The last point I wish to make is on the possibility of a commonwealth conference which has already been mentioned here today; and I wish to remind you again, Mr. Chairman, of what I quoted a few moments ago from the Minister of Trade and Commerce in which he spoke about what had been done by the United Kingdom. One would hope, not for a policy of restrictionism but a policy of liberalizing trade if and when such a conference is held.

Those, Mr. Chairman, are the comments I wish to make. I feel that we might well hope that the minister will, pursuant to what he did almost three months ago, let us know how the problem looks now from where he sits.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of inflicting a long speech on the committee at this stage of the proceedings, because after all we have had a number of discussions on monetary policy at the various stages of the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act.
However, there are a couple of matters I wish to draw to the attention of the minister, and a couple of problems which were raised on several occasions during the discussion on the Bank Act to indicate that certain happenings have created a situation which poses a rather serious problem.
I think the minister would agree that the grain growers of western Canada today are facing a very difficult situation, in part from the fact that a large amount of grain has not been sold and in part from the fact that there has been a serious drop in prices during the past year to the extent where the price of wheat has fallen by over 30 cents a bushel. That is not going to affect merely the grain growers. That situation is going to have an adverse effect upon the whole of Canada, because we know that when the prices of farm commodities decrease the sale of products of eastern Canada become seriously reduced in the west.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance stated that government intervention or expenditure is not a cure for the problems of those industries when supply has temporarily outrun demand at home and abroad. The basic solution for those industries must be to produce more efficiently, eliminate waste, reduce costs, and search for new markets. The minister's statement to that effect can be found at page 3727 of Hansard.
While I think we will all agree with the soundness of that statement, nevertheless I think the minister should also have added that the situation might require a change in government policy in order to meet that situation, and a change in certain government monetary policies. In so far as agriculture producing more efficiently is concerned, I believe they are producing as efficiently now as any other industry in this country. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture in their brief made, I believe, that statement, and I think their brief supports that contention. Consequently, I doubt very much whether it is possible for agriculture today to reduce their costs any further than they already have. They have eliminated labour
Supply-Finance
costs wherever possible by utilizing the most modern machinery and, from the experience I have had with agriculture, and it covers a period of around 40 years, I believe agriculture is operating very efficiently.
I would agree that somehow or other we will have to reduce agricultural costs in order to feed the world. The Minister of Agriculture, speaking before the FAO conference, stated that the cost of agricultural products in this country was so high that he doubted whether other countries could afford to buy them. If that statement is true, are we just going to sit down and lose our markets, or are we going to do everything in our power to make it possible for our agricultural products to compete with those of other nations in the world?
How could the minister help in that situation? There are two things that I think this government could do that would help agriculture in that matter; not only would it help agriculture but I think it would help all other exporters. First of all, there is the question of the value of the Canadian dollar.
Does the minister believe that it is really an advantage to the people of Canada to maintain the Canadian dollar at a level higher than that of the currency of any other country in the world? If our dollar was back to the level at which it was when it was 90 per cent of the United States dollar, the farmers would be receiving approximately another 20 cents a bushel for their wheat. Of course the same thing would be true with regard to other agricultural products that were exported.
The minister might argue that all other exporters are in the same position, but that is not quite true because the price of agricultural products in Canada is determined by the price at which they are sold abroad. That is not altogether true of secondary industries. They very often maintain two price systems. They sell at one price in Canada and at another price externally. But in Canada the domestic price of farm products is governed entirely by the external price. Therefore when a drop takes place abroad, the price of the commodity in Canada falls at the same time.
I do not think the minister would suggest that that is a matter that is beyond the control of the government. I think the minister would agree that there are many ways in which this government could control the value of the Canadian dollar. Of course I know he will say that if you drop the value of the Canadian dollar, it is going to cost us more for our imports. I think the main thing at the present time is to try to sell

Supply-Finance
more exports. In order to do that we have got to maintain our goods at competitive prices. At the present time we are having to compete with nations whose currency in every case is depreciated below United States currency. That fact has placed us in a very difficult position. Of course the United States is a competitor of ours. Our currency is even above that of the United States. That is one step that the government can take that I think would greatly help the agricultural exporter.
Then there is another matter which I think deserves consideration. It is one that I have raised many times in the House of Commons since 1945. I think probably my contention will bear more weight today because there are many more people today who realize the truth or the soundness of what we have advocated since 1945, namely that it is the responsibility of an exporting country to accept the currency of importing nations for a proportion of its exports.
The United States have been selling surplus farm products under the United States mutual security act since 1951, and the foreign currency they have accepted has been used for the purpose of financing defence projects. Now, however, they are considering going far beyond that. In the U.S. News and World Report I notice a statement showing that there is to be quite a change in the administration's policy with regard to the acceptance of sterling and other foreign currencies. I put this quotation on Hansard on June 15, as reported at page 5997. I am therefore not going to quote the whole thing at this time. It is interesting, however, to note that it is a disposal plan for farm surpluses and that it has received the administration's approval. Besides being utilized for financing defence projects it can be used for the following purposes:
In addition, the president would be authorized to use the foreign money for local improvements in the buying country, to pay U.S. obligations there, to buy military equipment, to help develop new markets for U.S. farm products, or for loans to promote world trade.
In fact, it could be used for almost anything. Now it points out that they expect to be able to have better trade with India because they would accept rupees instead of demanding American dollars. That policy is bound to affect the farmers in this country because we are having to compete with the United States in the sale of our commodities.
If the United States are going to sell their farm products to the other countries of the world and to accept their currencies instead of demanding American dollars whilst we in Canada insist upon their paying us in

Canadian dollars, it is quite easy to believe that many of those nations, lacking Canadian or American dollars, will buy from the United States instead of buying from Canada because they will have the wherewithal with which to buy. I hope the minister will be able to tell us whether or not any consideration is being given to that matter.
I suppose the minister might say we are doing it to a modified extent under the Colombo plan and that is true; under the Colombo plan we accept the currency of other nations, and then that currency is invested in projects within the country concerned. But that is only done to a modified degree, to the extent of some $25 million I believe. It therefore has little effect upon our trade as a whole.
The minister may say that we could not afford to do it and he may ask: What would we do with a lot of foreign currency? On the other hand I claim that where we have surplus goods that we cannot sell, we could very well afford to do it because if we do not sell those surplus commodities, what will happen? The producers of those surplus commodities are going to be told, as they are being told from day to day by the financial press, that they cannot expect to sell goods that are not wanted, that they must realize that in the final analysis there is only one law, namely the law of supply and demand. If therefore these producers are going to have to be governed by the law of supply and demand, there is only one thing that they can do and that is to reduce their production or cut their production down to the point where there will be a greater demand for their goods, so that the demand equals the reduced supply. Then the price will go up and the surplus will disappear. But if that is done, we lose those exports entirely.
It would be far better to export those goods at the present time and to accept foreign currencies for them rather than to reduce our production so that there are no surplus goods. I would say that for anyone to suggest that the solution is to cut our production is to take a defeatist attitude. It is taking the attitude that we have got to reduce our production in order to obtain a fair price. I think it would be far better to maintain our production at a high level so long as that production is needed in any part of the world. There is no question today that our production is needed. It is largely a matter of financing. If we are willing to do as the United States apparently are now doing, namely to accept the currency of other nations, I think we would find it much easier to dispose of our surplus commodities.

There is one other point I wish to refer to. A great deal of concern is being felt over the present price of agricultural products. I would point out to the minister that he cannot suggest that the farmers of this country should be prepared to compete with the farmers of other countries, because that is not the situation. The farmers of this country are not having to compete with the farmers of the United States. The farmers of this country are now having to compete with the United States treasury because the United States treasury is underwriting the price of farm products. When the United States cut the price of wheat by 10 cents a bushel it therefore was not the farmers that took that loss because the United States government has underwritten the price of wheat at $2.20 a bushel.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hate to interrupt my hon. friend, Mr. Chairman, but do we have to discuss wheat again on my estimates?

I am only discussing wheat to the extent that the price of wheat or the sale of wheat is affected by the policy of the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance can greatly affect the sale of wheat or any other commodity either by accepting foreign currency in payment or by changing the value of the Canadian dollar. We raised that matter in the banking and commerce committee. We asked Mr. Graham Towers whether or not he thought it would be advisable to reduce the value of the Canadian dollar. He said that was a matter that he would discuss only within four walls in giving advice to the government. He was not prepared to make a statement outside. The minister, however, represents the government. He is not under that same limitation. I hope he will be in a position either to justify maintaining the Canadian dollar at the present rate or to give us some indication that, in the near future, there will be removed the handicap which the farmers are under as a result of having to sell under an appreciated dollar. Those are the only two points I want to raise at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I feel I should perhaps say a word about what has been said by the two hon. members. I listened with a good deal of interest to what the hon. member for Greenwood had to say. By tradition I suppose it is possible to cover a fairly wide field on the first item of the estimates of any particular department. He certainly covered the waterfront.
I just tried to imitate the minister in a small way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not intend to imitate him in that respect. It is a tradition that once
Supply-Finance
a year the Minister of Finance makes a comprehensive and considered statement of the financial and economic position of the country and ventures into the field of prophecy. In the eight years that I have been Minister of Finance I have only ventured into that hazardous field once a year. I do not intend to break that precedent now. As a matter of fact I think it is undesirable that the minister should attempt from month to month to make new prophecies about the condition of the economy. If something radical happened it perhaps would be wise to try to give some indication, but I shall content myself with saying that nothing that has happened since I delivered my budget speech two or three months ago has caused me to change the qualified forecasts which I made in that speech.
The hon. member referred to the advances to the old age security fund. There again I dealt with that in my budget speech. I indicated that I expected there would be a further deficit in the coming year of somewhere between $40 million and $50 million and that under ordinary circumstances it perhaps would be prudent to increase the contribution in order to take care of that. I did say that it seemed to me this was not a year in which one should increase taxes if that could be avoided, and therefore I postponed making any recommendation.
The hon. member for Acadia has raised two points with which I will deal briefly. I agree with him it is extremely unfortunate that the price of one of our great export commodities, grain, wheat in particular, has fallen to the extent to which it has fallen. That has been dealt with at some length by my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is due, as we appreciate, to a series of big crops not only in this country but in other countries. The hon. member suggested that exports of wheat might be helped by a depreciation of the Canadian dollar. We have a free exchange now. The government does not attempt to influence the level at which the Canadian dollar is quoted in terms of other currencies. That is the position which we have taken since we freed the Canadian dollar in September of 1950.
I am not one of those who believe in the competitive depreciation of currencies. I believe that when a nation depreciates its currency the advantages are very short-run indeed. We had experience with fixed exchange rates and exchange controls over a considerable number of years. That was necessary, I think, under war conditions, but the experience after the war was not too happy. I am sure a good many members of the committee will recall the drastic

Supply-Finance
import restrictions which we had to put in effect in 1947 when we tried to defend the fixed exchange rate of the Canadian dollar at that time. I would hesitate to invite a repetition of that experience.
Therefore I do not believe that any action which the Canadian government might take to put a fixed exchange value on the Canadian dollar could possibly be successful without pretty drastic exchange controls. I for one would not be prepared to recommend at this time a return to that form of control.
As to taking sterling for our exports of wheat, that is not a new suggestion. Again, that was dealt with by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in the course of his remarks. I do not know of any country today in which we can sell substantial quantities of wheat for sterling, and certainly not in the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom is interested in the price of wheat but not in purchasing it for sterling. So far as India is concerned today, they are not buying wheat at all. They have notified the international wheat agreement that they do not want to take their quota. They have had a fine rice crop, a good grain crop, and they do not need wheat and are not going to buy any substantial quantity.
I understand the Poles are short of wheat, and we might take some Polish zlotys, if that is the currency that is prevalent in Poland, but I do not know just what we would do with them. I doubt if that would receive very widespread support. Taking foreign currencies for any commodity, which we do not need for purchases in the area from which we take it, is simply selling that commodity on credit and, as I have said before, assuming not only the credit risk but the exchange risk as well.
My hon. friend referred to United States sales for local currencies. I am told these are on a very limited scale. They have made some sales to Spain and they are going to use the proceeds in Spanish pesetas to pay for air bases in Spain. We are not building any air bases in Spain. I believe there are other modest sales of a similar character, but I am personally convinced that even if we were prepared to extend credit by selling for local currencies it would not substantially increase our sales of wheat. I do not know if there is any other point.

May I ask a question? The minister has read statements from time to time by officials of the United Kingdom blaming their reduction of purchases from Canada, especially farm products, on the fact that they have not got the dollars to pay for them. They may be just whistling

in the air, but they keep coming over here and making that statement. It has been made by a number of their representatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are trying to urge us to buy more in the United Kingdom. They would like to get into our market as a substitute for somebody else, and if they can do it competitively they can get in here. There is nothing to prevent them. They have a preference so far as tariffs are concerned over the United States, but they are not interested in buying wheat or any other commodity on credit today, whether it is in sterling or anything else.

Why would the United States be widening the use of foreign currencies if they did not think they were going to gain markets by doing so? According to a statement appearing in the U.S. News and World Report, they are going to widen the purposes for which foreign currencies can be used. They are not merely going to use them for investment in defence projects but utilize them for practically anything at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The information I have does not coincide with the information my hon. friend has read in the U.S. News and World Report.
It does not coincide with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

With respect to departmental administration, I notice there is an item for professional and special services which is a recurring item in most of the departmental accounts. Would the minister explain what kind of expenditure is covered by that item, professional and special services? I see the amount is $7,000 for this year, but there are no details in the public accounts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That provides for legal fees and court costs that may have to be paid by the Department of Finance in the coming fiscal year. That will include the expenses of court cases, if any, which have to be settled or disposed of under the old wartime prices and trade board administration and the foreign exchange control administration. We still have a number of those cases which are going through the courts, and that is what the item is intended to cover.
Mostly professional services.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.

In the absence of the hon. member for Hamilton West I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that whereas last year there were two office girls and one office boy on his general staff it

appears that this year there will be two office boys. I know that will not be very popular with the hon. member tor Hamilton West and is not in line with the practice of the department presided over by the acknowledged feminist, the Secretary of State. I notice he has one office girl whereas he had one office boy last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand the lady has been promoted. We still have her on strength but her remplacante is an office boy.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.

May I ask the minister
whether the functions of the farm loan board under the Farm Improvement Loans Act are determined-

Supply-Finance

Expenses of the Royal Canadian Mint and the assay office, Vancouver, B.C.-
110. Administration, operation and maintenance, $1,145,465.

This is always a very interesting operation, namely the operation of the mint. I think I read, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian government was minting a new nickel coin made of nickel. I wonder if the minister would give us an indication of how much it costs to make a nickel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I doubt if I have got that information. We are changing back to the five-cent coin made of nickel, which was discontinued when that material was in critical short supply. My information is that the changeback will be on January 1, next. As to the breakdown of the cost of making that coin, I doubt if we would have that breakdown. There is a profit. The mint operates at a profit, but I do not think we have the breakdown of cost as between minting subsidiary coins and the minting of 25 cent, 50 cent and one dollar silver pieces.

I take it there is a running account for it, an account for the silver and the nickel which is accredited with the value of the coinage that is minted and offset by the cost of minting and redeeming it. It would be interesting to know, within an approximate figure, how much it costs to make these new nickel coins.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I have not that detailed information here. I have no doubt it is available. I have some gross figures in the report of the Royal Canadian Mint, and no doubt my friend has seen them, for the calendar year 1953. There are some gross figures and the totals of expenditure which shows an excess of income over expenditure

Supply-Finance
for the mint as a whole of some $3,800,000. I have not a breakdown as between the individual mint operations.
I appreciate these coins have to be minted, but if I could just get that figure I should be happy to have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be happy to try and get it and send it to my friend.

Would this be the proper place to ask about the amount of gold bullion the government has accumulated and whether during the past year the government has accumulated all the newly mined gold submitted to it by the mines of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I believe that appears in the report of the exchange fund account. I have published those figures monthly, showing the proportion of gold. At the end of May, 1954, the official holdings of gold were $1,027-3 million, and the total gold processed for the mint in the calendar year 1953-I shall have to get that figure.
Practically all the newly mined gold, I take it, is being retained.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would think so, and perhaps a bit more. There is, of course, a small amount of gold that is sold on the free market, as my hon. friend knows. Then, there is a further amount that is supplied for the use of the arts. I have not a breakdown here as to the actual figure at the end of May.
Is there any gold purchased from any other source than Canadian producers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

To show how right the hon. member for St. Paul's was in saying how interesting the mint was, I might say that I had a school boy visiting me here. It was his duty to go back and report on what he had seen, and I was invited to be present. He gave a most eloquent speech all about the mint and did not even mention the fact that there was such a thing as the House of Commons here.
Inadvertently, Mr. Chairman, I missed the tariff board item. The minister, in his speech three months ago, indicated that applications were mounting and-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are we reverting to 109, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I called item 109 but I think the hon. member might raise his question now.

Can the minister say anything in addition to what he said in his

budget speech as to the indication of tariff-mindedness, let us say, arising. We have seen the minister's letter with regard to wool, and it may be he thinks that with that, and what he said in his budget speech, he has nothing to add. If he took that position, I would not press him, but if he could tell us anything more about it, we would be happy to hear it. We have been in the position for 15 years, really, of having tariffs, you might say almost, let out of our lives, with all their complexity. They seem to be coming back, and if the minister can say anything about it, it might be useful.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps this might be interesting to my hon. friend. Since 1949 the board has made a number of inquiries into customs tariff on subjects which have been referred by the Minister of Finance. At present there are four references before the board, the most recent one being the inquiry into woven woollen goods under tariff item 554B. Since 1949 the board has had 160 appeals lodged with it from decisions of the Department of National Revenue, of which 11 are still pending, and there are 10 I believe that have been appealed to the exchequer court. I believe it will be apparent the board has been pretty active in recent years.

To provide, subject to the approval of the treasury board, for miscellaneous minor and unforeseen expenses including authority to re-use any sums repaid to this appropriation from other appropriations, and special compensation or other rewards for inventions or practical suggestions for improvements, $1,000,000.

Yes; the Department of

other government departments using the Toronto switchboard service. The amount is $84,200. What is the mechanics of that arrangement?

Under what item would we discuss payroll costs, including superannuation payments? If it has been passed I would ask the minister about the increase in the contribution to the superannuation account. It was $16 million last year and it is $39 million this year, or an increase of about $22 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a statutory item, but I shall give an explanation. We have not yet reached it, but I shall have the information for the hon. member when we do reach it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Item 653 deals with superannuation, and I shall have one or two questions to ask when we reach it. Perhaps this information could be given then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have the information here. The substantial increase is mainly attributable to the influx of approximately 60,000 so-called temporary employees as contributors to the superannuation account. The remainder is attributable to such things as increased permanencies in 1953, promotions and the like. In classifying those persons as permanent, and making them eligible for

Supply-Finance
superannuation, the government had to pay into the fund an amount sufficient to cover the government's share.
Is the superannuation fund maintained for the federal civil service on a sound actuarial basis, or is it a fund that is being built up, and is not yet on a sound basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend will recall .-i am not sure whether he was in the house at the time-I tabled a report made by the Department of Insurance. That was the last actuarial report. It showed at that time a substantial deficit on an actuarial basis. The government is taking steps to correct that situation. We have paid into the fund, I believe, some $175 million toward making up the deficit, and have indicated that a further amount will be paid in as it becomes possible to do so. But in the meantime the full actuarial deficit is carried as a deficit, and the interest is paid each year-credited year by year-on that deficit. So I think it is quite correct to say that the fund is on an actuarially sound basis.

speechtext:

General administration-
652. Comptroller of the treasury-central office and branch offices administration-further amount required, $167,010.

I should like to ask a question about the university grants. I realize we have passed it, but I notice it is a little larger than last year. My information is that the total university population has been declining since war-veteran students have graduated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all the better for the universities, because the grant is based upon total population, not university population. It is 50 cents per head of population as determined by the bureau of statistics; and the grant is then divided among the eligible universities, based upon university enrolments. So that if there are a smaller number they would get a higher per capita amount.

If I might refer to the matter of university grants, I believe the national conference of Canadian universities recommended changing the base of payment from 50 cents per head of our population to a basis of $125 per student. The chief reason for this suggested change arises from the fact that the maritime provinces in particular are somewhat discriminated against on the present basis. I wonder if the minister has given consideration to this recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Various suggestions have been made, of course, that the base does operate

somewhat unfairly in respect of certain provinces. But on balance the government feels the present arrangement which is based on provincial population and enrolment in universities is as fair as can be worked out at this time.

Unfortunately, I was out of the chamber when item 113 was called.
I notice that last week when I was away, incidentally, the minister said, as reported at page 6047 of Hansard, in connection with the Municipal Grants Act:
When that Item is called we shall have an opportunity to discuss the matter and I can indicate, in a general way, the nature of the amendments which the government has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can revert to that for a moment. Perhaps I might say this to my hon. friend. There is something in excess of $3 million which will be paid out to various municipalities which qualify this fiscal year. I suppose it would be inappropriate for me to indicate in detail the provisions of the proposed legislation, but I can say this. It is estimated that it will involve an annual expenditure of something of the order of $6 million in all, and will approximately double the number of municipalities which will be eligible to receive a grant under the act. Other than that I do not suppose I had better say anything at this time. As I indicated in my statement, it would be available for the calendar year 1955.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
653. Superannuation and retirement acts, administration-further amount required, $13,837.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to say just a few words on item 653. First of all, I must confess that the last time I addressed a few words to the Minister of Finance on the plight of superannuated civil servants, namely, the great numbers of those already retired, I thought it would be the last time I would be doing so. I thought that by the time today rolled around the Minister of Finance might have left us. I am glad he is still with us. Mr. Abbott: Thank you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Since he is still with us, I hope he will even yet give consideration to this matter. I have no intention of repeating the many arguments-I think strong arguments-which I have given to the minister in years gone by since he first came into the Department of Finance as to why the government, as a model employer, should do something about the pensions of retired civil servants, particularly those in the lower brackets. I agree with his contention that the Public Service Superannuation Act, as

it now stands, is an excellent pension plan; certainly for those who are now in the public service the minister and the government have done well. But in the case of those who retired before the plan was put on its present excellent basis, and in the case of those who retired at such a time that their pension was calculated on the basis of the years when their rates of pay were very low, the situation is certainly nothing of which the government as an employer can be proud. I urge as strongly as I can once again that something should be done to supplement the pensions of those people.
The minister knows what the figures are, and people generally must know because I have put them on the record, and they have been published in the press a good many times. There are far too many of these faithful servants who are on pensions of $20, $30, $40 and $50 a month, which I submit is not good enough for the government of Canada.
One of the arguments the minister has advanced from time to time-I am going to confine myself today to just one argument and one reply to him-is that this pension is on the basis of a contractual relationship. He says that these people paid certain amounts into the fund at the time they were employed, and they knew what the arrangement was. He says that if you alter the amount of the pension now, it would upset that contractual arrangement. I submit, Mr. Chairman, there are other instances which are somewhat similar, where increases have been made.
I have told the minister about other governments and other private bodies until, if he has kept all the material I have given him, he must have quite a file on the matter. I want to give him one more example, one that I happen to know about in a personal way. Perhaps that is the reason I have not referred to it in the past. I happen to belong to a trade union, the International Typographical Union, which has a pension plan of its own, a very good pension plan, good enough at any rate that the Department of National Revenue has approved it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is going to have two pensions, then?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
As long as the Minister of Finance is around they will both be taxable, and as long as I stay in parliament I will not draw either of them.
In regard to the pension under the International Typographical Union, I would like to point this out. The amount of that pension used to be $10 a week or $520 a year. During the past ten years or twelve years it has been 83276-414
Supply-Finance
increased, step by step, until at the present time it is $20 a week or $1,040 a year. Does the minister suppose that that union pays the higher rate of pension only to those who have gone on pension since the rate was increased? Not a bit of it! That higher pension of $20 a week, or $1,040 a year, is paid to all of those who are on the pension, including those who went on it when it was only $10 a week, and including those who were contributing to it when the amounts paid into the fund were a great deal smaller than they are at the present time. I have given that example because it is one the details of which I happen to be familiar with. I know there are many other plans like that.
I want to say to the minister quite frankly that I do not think the government has a leg to stand on in insisting that it cannot do something for these people. If the minister wants to do something that will really give him a place in the hall of fame before he lays down the portfolio of finance, I suggest he pay some attention to the plight of these people and make some arrangement to increase the amount of the pensions of those already retired, particularly those in the lower brackets.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no purpose in my rehashing the points which I have made before. Whatever may be done under the International Typographical Union pension plan-I am sure it is very generous-we are dealing with taxpayers' money here. These things have to be paid for out of taxes levied on all the taxpayers of Canada, and a great many of those who have had to provide for their old age by contractual arrangements or otherwise do not get any automatic increase in their pensions, with this exception, that we have introduced in the last few years the old age pension plan of $40 at age 70. Most of those pensioners to whom my hon. friend refers are very elderly people, people whose small pensions are due to the comparatively short time of their service in the public service. They benefit from the $40 old age pension, payable at age 70. That, incidentally, does not apply to some of the countries to which he has referred where civil servants' pensions were increased.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I want to add one word, Mr. Chairman. The minister says that this has to be paid for out of the money of the taxpayers. The plan to which I have referred is paid for out of the money contributed by the members of the union. What happens in that case is that the older members who contributed smaller amounts in years gone by are getting larger pensions now because those who are now working are paying in

Supply-Finance
larger amounts. I am proud to belong to a union that recognizes that principle, and I should like to see this government, and society as a whole, recognize it, too.

I would like to say a word on this item. I recall last year there was discussion along this line on one particular problem. It was a rather extended discussion at the time and it related to the peculiar position of the former employees of the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment and the soldier settlement board. I followed the discussion last year with a good deal of interest, as did a good many hon. members in this chamber. Apparently the arguments that were put forward impressed the minister because he promised to give the matter serious consideration. The crux of the problem is that the employees of these two departments were not in a position to become permanent employees because of a policy decision and as a result they did not benefit on the five-year basis for superannuation, which is the right of superannuated civil servants under part II of the superannuation act of 1924. The minister made the statement that if any erroneous decision had been made he would be glad to consider the whole situation and if he became convinced that any substantial injustice in principle had been done he would be glad to give consideration to ways and means of redressing it. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I promised last year that I would have a very extensive individual investigation made of these cases. In essence I can sum it up by reading the last two paragraphs:
After giving careful consideration to all arguments that have been advanced, I cannot be persuaded that the Public Service Superannuation Act leaves any substantial injustices in principle unremedied. The basis of the Civil Service Superannuation Act was that to enjoy the benefit of the five-year average salary in calculating the allowance a person had to be a civil servant within the meaning of the act on July 19, 1924. No evidence has been advanced to show that the employees in question were permanent then and any action which might have been taken to provide for them at the time, while considered, was not, in fact, taken. Thus they, along with the thousands of other temporary employees in 1924, have come under the ten year average salary for superannuation purposes.

While it is true that this is the only case of which I know where a department has been excluded
almost as a whole,-
That was the old department of soldiers' civil re-establishment.
-yet it never was made a permanent department. Even if it were decided that something should be done for those employees whom the department thought should have been made permanent in 1924, how can one be sure how many would, in fact, have been. One brief on behalf of these employees has, in fact, requested that all of them be given the benefit of the five year average which, if granted, would have been altogether unfair to all other temporary employees in 1924.
I have come to the conclusion, therefore, that I cannot recommend to the government that this benefit of the use of the five-year average salary in determining superannuation benefits be conferred on these employees.
If my hon. friend would like to have it I would be happy to send him a rather more extensive memorandum breaking down the number of individual cases, and so on.

I thank the minister for that statement. There is just one other point. The minister will probably recall that the emphasis during the discussion last year was not on the legal right as defined by the act, but on the moral right. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Here again, Mr. Chairman, the difficulty was that this was considered in 1924, 1925 and 1926 and during the early thirties, and it was rejected. Combines Investigation Act-
168. Restrictive trade practices commission, $71,668.

I want to pause at item 168 for a moment because I think it is important that we should discuss investigations now being carried on by the restrictive trade practices commission into the subject of loss leaders. The whole situation arises out of legislation which was passed here in December, 1951, and which eliminated the only protection the retail trade of Canada had at that time against this practice, that is against the loss-leader practice. We gave quite extensive warnings to the government, on behalf of the retail trade, that there was then an imminent danger that if the protection of resale price maintenance was removed, many retailers would be ruined by resort to the loss leader and to other unfair competitive practices which had been previously followed and against which the device of resale price maintenance was worked out largely by the retail trade itself.
We now find, Mr. Chairman, that the loss-leader practice has, in fact, assumed the serious proportions which we forecast at that time, in 1951. It has unfortunately to be recorded that the government to date has taken no action whatsoever to deal in a positive way with the threat which the loss-leader practice presents to the retail trade. They have taken certain preliminary steps in that they have asked the restrictive trade practices commission to investigate and consider the matter. Recently the commission has commenced public hearings. I understand that those hearings will not be concluded for a month or two yet. We are therefore faced with the situation that nothing can be done until that report comes in, and presumably nothing effective can be done until this fall, if parliament should meet in November. Hence it is probably not until at least early next year that the retailers can expect any action to protect them against what is going on.
I want to ask the minister to let us know what the thinking of the government is with respect to this matter and to give us an

indication, if he can, of the action it is proposed to take and how soon it is proposed to take it when the report is made.
I do this because the figures with regard to commercial failures are quite disturbing. I do not wish to be taken as suggesting, because it is not my intention, that the trend shown by the increased number of commercial failures results exclusively from the legislation passed in 1951 and from the subsequent reappearance of the loss-leader practice. But I do suggest that when we find on the one hand that the retail trade itself is convinced, and has stated so publicly on a number of occasions, that this loss-leader practice is closely tied up with commercial failures, and when we find on the other hand a disturbing increase in the number of commercial failures, we are justified, and unfortunately justified, in saying that the forecast which we made in 1951 is now being fulfilled.
What we said in 1951 was that the retailers required some protection against the loss-leader practice and if that protection was not given it would have disastrous results on the retail trade. The government took a much more sanguine view. They said: Oh well, we do not think the loss-leader practice will ever recur under existing economic conditions but if it does we will consider it then and we will be in a position to do something about it. I obtained recently from the bureau of statistics tables of figures showing the number of commercial failures in Canada for every year since 1949, and I should like to put them on the record because they substantiate what I have said to the effect that there is a disturbing situation in that regard.
The first figures I shall give are for all types of commercial failures in Canada reported under the provisions of the Bankruptcy and Winding Up acts. There were 1,045 in 1949, 1,275 in 1950, 1,349 in 1951, 1,434 in 1952 and 1,617 in 1953. It will be seen that while these figures do not establish conclusively that the current increase in commercial failures results from the legislation of 1951, nevertheless there has been a disturbing increase in the last two years and an increase of 183 in 1953 over 1952.
In attempting to relate this specifically to the retail trade I was told by the bureau of statistics that they do not have the figures in that form but they do have a subdivision for "total trade" which they tell me would be mainly retail establishments. The record of failures under that subheading shows the same increase in 1953 over 1952. The situation is even more alarming if you compare the first quarters. I should point out that
Supply-Justice
the figures for 1954, the current year, are only complete up to the end of the first quarter. They show a very much more disturbing increase in the number of failures in the first quarter this year over the first quarter last year. They also show a steady increase in the first quarter of each year since the first quarter of 1951. They do show a drop in 1953, but that trend seems to have been reversed at the present time. The total figures for the first quarter of every year from 1949 are as follows: 270 for 1949, 382 for 1950, 402 for 1951, 470 for 1952, 382 for 1953 and 680 for 1954.
Taking the subheading of "total trade", which is as near as the bureau can come with respect to the retail trade figures, the figures for the first quarters of each of these years, 1949 to 1954, are as follows: 93 in 1949, 149 in 1950, 168 in 1951, 186 in 1952, 146 in 1953 which is a slight drop, and then an alarming increase to 299 for the first quarter of 1954. I put these figures on the record to show that a discussion of the position of the retail trade and the impact on that trade of the loss leader practice is not one which is carried on in the realm of abstraction. It is a very concrete and disturbing situation that we are dealing with.
That of course is borne out by the statements of the retail trade itself. I have followed the press reports of the representations made to the restrictive trade practices commission in the course of its public hearings. I have not seen all the briefs and I can only assume and accept these press reports as representing accurate summaries of the presentation. I should like to place before the committee some of the views expressed by the retailers either individually or by association spokesmen, as reported-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Were these views expressed by retailers or other commercial concerns which had failed, or were they views expressed by retailers generally?

The views I am now coming to are those of retailers generally. I do not think any of those who appeared before the commission were in fact bankrupt or had failed. That I do not know. That does not appear from the articles. As I read the articles, they were representations made by merchants continuing in business or else by trade associations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member is not citing these quotations as proving his point as to the cause of any failures that took place?

I certainly am. In the extracts which I shall read I will be quoting opinions to the effect that the re-emergence of the loss-
