leader practice has a very direct bearing on the number of commercial failures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but these are not the explanations of merchants who themselves have failed.

That I am not able to state conclusively. I do not think any of the representations I shall be quoting were made by people who had in fact failed. Some of them may have been, but I do not think so. This is a report that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of June 2, 1954 and it deals with the hearings held in Toronto. It reads in part as follows:
John Jardine, a spokesman for the Canadian sporting goods and cycle association, said large department and chain stores "seem bent on putting the small merchants out of business. We are meeting prices in what I am sure is a suicide race", he said. "If we don't maintain these prices we are sure to go out of business."
The wholesale hardware association urged a return of legislation to stop loss leader selling.
Then there is a reference to another spokesman, Fred R. Cavers of St. Catharines, Ontario. I have not had an opportunity to look up the genealogical tree of this gentleman, but I point out that his name bears a resemblance to that of one of the members of the house. He comes from St. Catharines, Ontario, and I think that city is very near the constituency represented by the hon. member whom I have in mind. The report reads:
Fred R. Cavers of St. Catharines, Ontario, speaking for electrical appliance dealers, condemned cut price sales on vacuum cleaners and television sets in his area as "vicious and predatory business practices". Cavers claimed some merchants were advertising "nailed down loss leaders", yet fining a salesman $5 if he sold the bargain item instead of "using it as a come-on" after getting customers in the store.
That refers to the criticism made by reputable retailers that a brand-name article will be advertised at a cut price, lower than the price for which neighbouring stores are selling it, as a come-on to get the customer in the store. But when the customer is in the store he is told: Oh, I am sorry, but the last of those was sold five minutes ago, but we have so and so and such and such which we assure you is every bit as good. But the customer finds the price is quite different. That is all tied up with the loss leader practice, which does not help the consumer.
Another presentation made before the commission in Montreal, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of June 8, was made on
IMr. Fulton.]
behalf of the Quebec retail tobacco association by Mr. H. J. Garfinkel, honorary president of the association. His presentation is summarized as follows:
Mr. Garfinkel said the last defence of the retailer had been demolished with abolition of price maintenance-the selling of goods at uniform prices by all retailers.
The small retailer's profit on cigarettes, he added, had not been excessive. It was a little more than
3	cents in 1939 for a 20-cent package and not quite
4	cents for the present-day 33-cent pack.
But if the small retailers were to compete with chain stores, he said, they actually would have to take a loss of a tenth of a cent a pack.
The large stores, the brief continued, selling cigarettes only as an incidental, can afford to take this loss if it brings in customers for other goods. But the small tobacconists depend on cigarettes for more than two-thirds of their sales.
He went on to describe the emergence of bankruptcy in some very large tobacco retail concerns in the United States and said:
Only definite action on dominion, provincial, or municipal levels can save the Canadian tobacconist from the same fate.
There was another presentation on the following day, June 9, reported in the Gazette, by Mr. F. G. Samis, commercial manager of the Northern Electric Company. The report reads as follows:
Mr. Samis included among predatory price-cutters retailers selling goods at a loss as a come-on for other products. He said all price-cutting was not bad, naming progressive price-cutting and protective price cuttings as ethical practices.
Price maintenance would allow these methods, he explained, but would prevent price wars.
George Pynn, appliance manager for Northern Electric, said in reply to a question he did not know of any manufacturer who had dropped a retailer cutting prices for justifiable reasons.
Then, the last report I have, and I think it was the last session of the commission in Montreal, is taken from the Montreal Gazette of June 11 and reports the presentation made by the radio-television manufacturers association of Canada as follows:
A member of the association's delegation, Harry Marpole, of the R.C.A. Victor Company of Canada, later said bankruptcy was up considerably among his company's retail dealers since the government had removed price maintenance.
"We have experienced", he said, "in the last twelve months, approximately 10 times the number of bankruptcies among our dealers as the average of the five years preceding that period."
He said the cause was that dealers were forced to sell at prices that were too low for their budgets.
He said he did not think there had been overproduction of television sets by his company last year.
Another witness who was heard at the time of this presentation was Mr. L. P. Fournier, credit manager of the Gerin, Trudeau Company. The report states that he-
-warned that unless price maintenance was reestablished many persons of bankrupt businesses would become unemployed.

They in turn would become dependent on public support paid for by the consumers whom the abolition of price maintenance was intended to help in the first place.
I have read those quotations, Mr. Chairman, to establish that in the view of the retailers, based upon their experience, and in the view of manufacturers who supply retailers, the re-emergence of the loss-leader practice has had exactly the result it was feared it would have by retailers at the time when protection against it was eliminated in 1951. The results which we forecast this would have, unless the government brought in some concurrent arrangements which would enable the retailer to protect himself in that regard, are exactly what has happened. I should be clear on that. What has happened is what we forecast. The government did not take any action when it removed the protection, and the disastrous consequences to the retailer have followed.
What about the consumers?

My hon. friend asks about the consumer. I have some tables here which show to what extent the consumers may have benefited. I know that the figures are rather dangerous, and I said that although the figures show an alarming increase in the number of commercial failures, I am not prepared to say that that is entirely or exclusively attributable to the 1951 legislation. In the same way I hope that my hon. friends will not say that any reduction in the cost of living has been entirely attributable to that 1951 legislation. If they do make that argument, then I still do not think they could take very much comfort from it because the reduction is so small as to be virtually negligible.
The figures for the consumer price index are as follows:	On January 1, 1952, 118-2;
January 1, 1953, 115-5; January 1, 1954, 115-7 and on May 1, 1954, 115-7. It will be seen that in the three year period there has been a reduction in the consumer price index of 2-5 points. If my hon. friends are going to take much comfort out of that, then they can attribute the whole of it, if they like, to the action taken by the government in 1951. I still do not think it will comfort them very much, nor will it comfort the consumer. The consumer will be as disturbed as we are by what is happening to the small merchant in Canada as a result of the loss of protection he is now experiencing.
I should like to review for a moment what was said back in 1951, and show that not even the action forecast by the government has yet been taken. As reported on page 2451 of Hansard for December 28, 1951, we pointed out to the government this was a danger to the retail trade and we asked them what they proposed
Supply-Justice
to do about it. Perhaps I could ask the indulgence of the committee while I read some remarks which I made on that occasion, because I want to show how clearly we warned the government as to what might happen. Discussing this situation I said, as reported at page 2451 of Hansard for December 28, 1951:
The proof of what I am saying is found in the statement of the Prime Minister yesterday when, as set out at page 2335, he was attempting to justify the government's willingness to rush the small retailers of Canada into oblivion, and leave with a few big giants of industry the control of the distribution of goods in this country. He said:
"I made the statement the other day, and I repeat it, that if as a result of this legislation or as a result of any other condition there develops a contrary abuse, the government will consider what recommendations it should make to parliament to deal with that contrary abuse."
He was referring to the possibility of the loss-leader practice. Well, I would ask the Prime Minister or, since he is not in his seat, the Minister of Justice, just how long he thinks it will take to consider and work out that recommendation? At what stage will the government decide that it has become necessary to work out some alternative form of protection? How many retailers will have to go to the wall? How many bankruptcies will have to take place in Canada? How many small concerns will have to be taken over by the giants of the distributive trades before the government decides the time has come at which they must give consideration to some alternative form of protection for the small retailer? Will it be one, or twenty-one, or a hundred or five hundred? How many thousands will have to be lost by small retailers before the government decides it is time to act?
The minister referred me to a statement he had made previously but which, as I pointed out to him, was not an answer to that particular question. At a later stage, at the top of page 2496 of Hansard for that day, the minister did say that the government would act quickly if a serious situation developed. He said that if the loss-leader practice emerged, and if it assumed serious proportions, then they would look very carefully at section 498A of the Criminal Code to see if something could be done. We asked him if that had been effective, and he said in his knowledge it had only been used once, so that is where that matter was left.
However, at an earlier stage he said that the government-perhaps I had better read the quotation from page 2496:
Should it become apparent that section 498A is not adequate to deal with any abuse of that sort which might make its appearance, then we are in a position, because of the work which has already been done, to follow out quite quickly any policy which might be agreed upon by the government at that time. But our own view coincides with that of the committee, that as long as present economic conditions continue there is no substantial likelihood of widespread predatory price cutting or loss leaders.
I think that is all I need to quote from the previous debate. What I have quoted

Supply-Justice
proves conclusively that the government was warned that this loss-leader practice would re-emerge. They said they did not believe that it would re-emerge, but that if it did they would be in a position to act quickly as a result of the work which had already been done.
Yet we find this serious situation confronting the retail trade of Canada, where they are being very substantially prejudiced by this practice. And what has the government done? As I pointed out earlier, it has done nothing of a positive nature. After having said they would be in a position to act quickly, the best they have been able to do is to instruct a commission to consider the matter, to hold public hearings and to bring in a report.
I suggest it is a fair inference to draw from what was said by the Minister of Justice in 1951, that the government intended us to understand at that time that it would be ready to act quickly, and that it would not be necessary for it to go about the country three years later inquiring into the matter and asking retailers to state facts which are already known; that is, that they are now suffering, and suffering severely, as a result of what was done in 1951, and as a result of that action not being accompanied by the corresponding action we asked for in 1951, to enable them to provide their own protection against the loss-leader practice.
I have made this brief review of the situation because I believe the House of Commons and the country should now hear from the minister just what the government proposes to do by way of action to protect the retail trade. And I say this because I do not believe there is anyone in the house or in the country who, if he stops to think, will not agree with me when I say that there is no more important group of people in Canada and in the maintenance of a sound economy than the small and independent retail dealers.
We believe that the health of the economy is indicated by the number of people who are self-employed, and gainfully employed, in commercial pursuits of one kind or another. We do not believe that it is either safe or healthy to see developing a tendency where the small and independent man goes to the wall, and his place is taken by the giant concern, with an inevitable drift toward a situation where everybody will be the employee of somebody else. Where everybody is an employee of somebody else, it means you will have a few giant concerns in the country for whom, in the long run, far too many people work. And it is that danger and that trend we are concerned to see dealt

with. And it is because of the desirability of preserving in Canada the maximum number of small and independent concerns that I say the government is bound at this time to indicate what action it intends to take to protect those interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend's case seems to be that, inasmuch as he alleges that commercial failures are on the increase, and that they follow the government's legislation in 1951 banning resale price maintenance that therefore the legislation is the cause of the commercial failures. This is the ancient and hoary fallacy of post hoc, ergo propter hoc- because B follows A, therefore A is the cause of B; or because A is associated with B, therefore one is the cause of the other.
Would the minister permit me-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend may deal with it when I have finished.
The minister has misinterpreted and distorted my argument. But I will correct it later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Moreover while I reject this reasoning completely, I reject with greater vehemence the premise upon which it is based.
Tell us what you are going to do for the retailer.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that I could tell my hon. friend anything, but if he will let me make my speech I will endeavour to explain my own viewpoint.
To begin with my hon. friend has quoted figures from an unimpeachable source as establishing the commercial failures in Canada. But if he had examined those figures with a little greater care he would have seen that the bankruptcies included those estates, whether commercial or otherwise, which are under $500 in value, after deducting claims of secured creditors. He would also find there is a very heavy element in the figures he quoted of estates of wage earners where the assets of the estate are $500 or less, after deducting the claims of secured creditors.
For example, in the first three months of 1953 the total number of estates were 375, and out of that total number there were 178 bankruptcies in which the value of assets, exclusive of preferred claims, was less than $500. By no stretch of the imagination could all these, many of which involved wage earners, be regarded as commercial failures. Thus even if my hon. friend argued more logically than he did, he could not fail, since he started from a false premise, to reach a fallacy, and that is what he has reached.

Now, my hon. friend has raised this question at a time when this matter of loss leaders is under consideration by the restrictive trade practices commission. This commission is going about the country hearing from those sources from which my hon. friend quoted, commercial organizations of one kind or another who are opposed to the government legislation, and hearing also from sources from which my hon. friend did not quote, the Canadian Association of Consumers, for example, who are supporting the government legislation.
Until that report is brought in I think perhaps he would agree that the best course we could follow in this chamber is to await the considered view of the commission-the considered view which I am sure it will bring forth. My hon. friend from Kamloops is alleging that the increase in bankruptcies is the result of these loss leaders that he is complaining about. How does he explain that there is a higher number of bankruptcies in the case where there has been relatively little price cutting, as compared with a lower number of bankruptcies in another industry where there has been a greater amount of it? By every test that one can apply to both his facts and his reasoning, his case is disproven by his own arguments, and certainly disproven by studies such as the one by Dun and Bradstreet, to which I have made reference.

Mr. Chairman, this debate today recalls to the minds of those of us who were in the House of Commons in December, 1951, the debate at that time which occupied some days in the house after the matter of resale price maintenance had been considered at some length in a committee of the house. It recalls an episode in which the government with great haste sought to perpetrate a hoax upon the consumers of Canada, and to seize upon a scapegoat in the form of the practice of resale price maintenance as the means by which that hoax would be perpetrated upon the consuming public of Canada.
This legislation which was enacted in December, 1951, came at a time when prices were rising swiftly in this country and when the effects of a rapidly rising cost of living were being keenly felt by the consuming public of Canada. The government was a party to the rapid rise in the cost of living

for in that year the government, not satisfied with an already too high burden of taxation which it had imposed upon the Canadian people, chose that very time to increase the burden of taxation, particularly those taxes which entered into the cost of living. That was the year in which they raised the sales tax from 8 per cent to 10 per cent. That was the year in which they raised the excise tax on many commodities that entered into the cost of living of the average Canadian household up to figures like 25 per cent and 35 per cent. That was the year in which they applied excise taxes up to 15 per cent on many commodities on which no excise tax had been levied up to that time.
We now see chickens coming home to roost in this year 1954. In December 1951 the government sought to fool the Canadian people. They sought to make the Canadian public believe that the practice of resale price maintenance was contributing to this soaring increase in the cost of living that plagued the consuming public at that time. The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that the legislation then passed, which had the effect of banning resale price maintenance, contributed nothing to lowering the cost of living. Indeed, before the inquiry conducted in the fall of 1951 in committee had run its course, the Prime Minister had given the government's whole case away.

Can we get on with the business, Mr. Chairman?
I was saying that the chickens are coming home to roost. The fact is that it may have been relatively easy, as the government surveyed the situation in December, 1951, to expect that they would get away with what they were doing, because we then had a situation where there was a sellers' market; people could sell virtually whatever they had to sell. Therefore the problem of the loss leader, which is inherent in this question, did not arise in pressing form. However, in June, 1954, we have a far different situation. Competition is infinitely keener today than it was two and a half years ago. In the retail trade as well as in industry and commerce generally in this country the situation is far different. We can see arising now, Mr. Chairman, the effects that were inevitable in this legislation. It took time for those effects to demonstrate themselves, but they are demonstrating themselves today. The practice of the loss leader-a vicious practice, if ever there was one-was inevitable following upon the legislation of December, 1951.
That question of finding some way of dealing with the vicious practice of the loss leader did engage the committee that wrestled with this subject, and I recall that some hon. members opposite-the hon. member for Spadina, for instance-did try to come to grips with what they realized was a problem that would inevitably arise, namely, the loss-leader practice. They were not able to work out any satisfactory legislative formula to deal with the problem of the loss leader. That, sir, is the inherent weakness and defect of the legislation that was passed in December, 1951.
The government, determined to carry "through the project on which it had started -at that time, that hoax I have referred to, was prepared to go ahead willy-nilly, recklessly, and to see to it that legislation passed [DOT]without having put before parliament any Satisfactory legislative formula to prevent the rise of the loss-leader practice. The fact is that efforts were made at that time to devise some legislation to deal with the problem of the loss leader, but nobody was able to come up with a satisfactory legislative formula to deal with it.
But the government was not to be deterred. Loss of face was one thing they would not brook. The Minister of Justice was quite concerned at that time in trying to appear to do something in this field of competition to help the public, forgetting that he was the man -who had suppressed for ten long months in

defiance of the law of this country the McGregor report on the alleged milling combine. When the minister talks today about his belief in free enterprise, tries to make the rafters ring in this chamber, and says that he acts according to his belief, let me recall to his apparently deficient memory the fact that nobody who has held the portfolio of justice has done any more to weaken the system of free enterprise or the people's belief in it than was done by his wilful and illegal suppression of the McGregor report on the alleged milling combine.
The situation that we see today arising out of keen competition is the kind of situation which brings about a resurgence of the loss-leader practice. The Minister of Justice has not denied today the resurgence of the loss-leader practice. Indeed, he could not. It is known by everyone who has any knowledge of current commercial practices, particularly in the retail field, that the loss-leader practice is flourishing today and is doing very great harm to the legitimate retail trade. That, indeed, is the reason the Minister of Justice appointed this commission. He waited two and a half long years until the chickens had come home to roost, until this vicious practice was flourishing again, before he took any steps to initiate an inquiry into it.
Nobody quarrels with his institution of an inquiry. What we deplore is that he waited for two and a half long years to set up this inquiry. The warnings were there, given to him in December, 1951, but he just would not listen to them, and he has waited until this evil practice has flourished again before he has taken even this elementary step of beginning an inquiry into the practice. The practice is in existence. He knows it. He has been dilatory in the face of the revival of a vicious practice, a practice whose return was inevitable once parliament passed the legislation that this government imposed upon it in December, 1951.
The retail difficulties are all there today. The practice of loss-leader selling is wreaking its havoc in the Canadian retail trade. It is not confined to any one particular commodity. It has become quite widespread in the Canadian retail trade. Mr. Chairman, prior to the dinner recess there had been some discussion indicating that there might possibly be a difference of opinion between the two sides of this house as to what may be cause and what may be effect in the present situation. Now, we may not agree on the causes, but we can agree, surely, on the effects as we see them today. And those effects are a revival, in a flourishing condition, of the vicious practice of the loss leader. And, so far as cause is concerned, whether the practice itself has brought on much or little of the present condition, the fact is that the present condition in the Canadian retail trade, one of increasingly keen competition, is the kind of situation in which the loss-leader practice was bound to be revived. And that has followed; and we say it has followed inevitably. It followed because of the enactment of the legislation in December 1951 at the behest of the government. Had that legislation not been enacted we would see today the benefits of the practices that had, before that time, eliminated the loss-leader practice from Canadian retail selling.
There are those who profess to see advantages to the consumer in a situation of this kind. Well, of course there are advantages to the consumer in a competitive situation such as we have today. Wherever you have a buyers' market, as at the present time, naturally there are advantages to the consumer-just as in December 1951, in the midst of a sellers' market the seller did possess an advantage in dealing with the consumer.
But it would be a very great mistake to think that the practice we are complaining about now, this evil loss-leader practice, has brought benefit to the Canadian public. Competition may be-and I have indicated that it is-of advantage to the Canadian consumer. But it is a very different thing to say that the loss-leader practice works to the advantage of the consumer.
There may be thought to be some shortterm advantages to the consumer in the loss-leader practice. Some consumers think that there are bargains to be had under these conditions. Well, as hon. members who have had experience in retailing well know, the fact of the matter is that the first victim of the loss-leader practice is the consumer himself, as a class.
These so-called price wars are in many cases simply fictitious. The loss leader that is put out and becomes a bait for attracting the unsuspecting public into the retail store
[The Chairman.]
is put on sale at only short intervals, then withdrawn, and more expensive merchandise is put in its place. These are but some of the phases of the loss-leader practice which have been exposed whenever inquiries have been held, whether in this country or elsewhere. And in the 308-page volume published in April following an inquiry made by the restrictive trade practices commission, at the request of the Minister of Justice, we see catalogued on page after page these iniquitous phases of the practice of loss-leader selling.
I am sure no one in the house will have the temerity to justify or defend the loss-leader practice. It is vicious from start to finish, and in every respect. And the extent to which the loss-leader practice flourishes marks also the extent to which the small retailer is placed in jeopardy, because the effect of this practice inevitably and invariably has been to concentrate retail business in the larger outlets at the expense of the small retailer.
From what I have seen of it of late in Toronto, it is the small retailer-in many cases the young veteran who established himself in business since the war-who is feeling most keenly the effects of the loss-leader as practised by larger retailers.
So let no one try to justify this practice, as though it were of some benefit to the consumer. The consumer is the person who will lose out in the long run by reason of the curtailment of retail outlets and the gradual submergence of the small retailer in favour of the concentration of business in the hands of the larger retailer.
Finally, I offer one word in reference to legislation in the United States. This afternoon the minister made some reference to this subject and sought to draw an inference from it which I suggest is not warranted, and which is not particularly material to the point at issue. It is undoubtedly a fact that there are bankruptcies in the United States in retail trade today. But in those cases it is part of the general picture of meeting competition. It is part of the general condition that exists in the retail trade today. In their case it is not the result of legislation which opens the way for the loss-leader practice.
In 45 of the 48 states of the American union there is legislation commonly called fair trade legislation which permits resale price maintenance and thus combats the loss-leader practice. The constitutionality of that legislation was upheld by the Supreme Court of the United States when it refused leave to

appeal from a decision affirming the constitutionality of this state legislation. Something of this kind would be altogether desirable in this country.
There must be legislation, Mr. Chairman, which will make it possible for business to be cleansed of the loss-leader practice. Can it be done by a legislative enactment which will specifically prohibit the loss-leader practice? Well, all that I can say on that subject is this. Out of the experience of sitting in that committee in the autumn of 1951 and through the debates of this house which preceded and followed the sittings of the committee, all I can say is that at that time at any rate no member of the committee, no member of the house, no adviser of the Department of Justice was able to bring forward a satisfactory enactment to prohibit the practice of loss-leader selling.
The hon. member for Spadina attempted to write such a section in the committee. It was found, in the view of the committee, not to offer a workable solution. If the commission that the Minister of Justice has set up and is now holding sittings is able to bring forward some legislative formula to prohibit the loss-leader practice then they will have done something that nobody has been able to do effectively up to the present time. In truth, Mr. Chairman, the effective antidote to the loss leader, the vicious loss-leader practice, is the kind of practice within industry which was permitted under the laws that existed prior to December 1951, and which is prohibited today by legislation enacted by this parliament at the request of the government.
While I have no wish to prejudge the findings of the commission I will say this, Mr. Chairman. It seems to me that if they are being asked to write a legislative provision prohibiting specifically the loss-leader practice, they have been assigned an impossible task. It will have to be left to other methods to grapple with this vicious practice, and I for my part express my regret that the government, for partisan reasons, in 1951 denied to business the opportunity of cleansing the retail trade in this country from the vicious loss-leader practice.

It might be interesting to the minister to get a little firsthand information pertaining to the loss-leader business. I happen to be one of those small merchants who unwittingly found himself enmeshed in these very tactics. I have been running a retail business for a number of years. I have always run it on a live and let live principle. I enjoy quite a considerable patronage in our town. It is only a small town of about 1,600 or 1,700 people. We had two other meat merchants there. We have a nice business and are doing it legitimately. Just about the
Supply-Justice
time that I was elected to come to Ottawa a very fine supermarket was set up in our town. I know that most people who are familiar with the meat business know that the hamburger trade is perhaps the same to the retail butcher as the cough drops are to the Smith Brothers. It is very important. As a matter of fact, you cannot survive without it. I enjoyed a very large trade. I gave them the very best that was to be had. It was always fresh and good, and the price was always right. Therefore I obtained about 90 per cent of all the hamburger business in our town. I have 95 per cent of all the restaurant and hotel business. It was very important business.
So far as the hamburger was concerned, I was selling it pretty well on a break-even basis. But this famous unit came to town and perhaps they felt that the hamburger level was most vulnerable so far as my business was concerned, and they concentrated on that. The result was they were quoting hamburger at less than 25 cents a pound. They were paying the same as I was, 37 cents and 39 cents a pound for beef. You can see the effect that would have on legitimate trade.
I believe the retail merchants serve a very useful purpose in a community. We enjoy the confidence and the support, not only of the people of the town but of people from quite a distance away from the community. They were quite happy and satisfied. As a matter of fact in the twelve years or thirteen years that I have been there my business has increased about thirteen times what it was when I bought it in the spring of 1942. That should be proof enough that the people must have felt they were getting a square deal. This unit came to town with perhaps a hundred times as much money as I had, and they viciously tried to put the skids under my business as well as under the other gentlemen who were doing a legitimate business in our town. If you need any evidence, I can give it to you. I can tell you where to go and get that evidence. There is no monkey or no funny business about this; it is a reality.
I sincerely hope it will not result in two or three more cases of bankruptcy because of unfair tactics from that angle. I am not pleading particularly for myself. I am not afraid of legitimate business. I happen to be mayor of that town. I am serving my fifth term there now. I have never yet tried to discourage anyone from coming in there and opening up in opposition to my own business or to any other business. When people come to a town and make a gentleman's agreement that they are going to do business on the level and then they come out with those tactics, it is about time that this government or somebody started to reckon with that kind of condition.

Supply-J ustice
What I am saying goes for small merchants in our town or anywhere else. If I am going to be steamrollered and pushed aside because big business likes to come in there and steamroller us out of business, it is about time that this government took some action in the matter. I am not particularly in favour of price controls. I have worked under price controls and I do not relish them too much, but the minister would be well advised to consider ways and means of keeping this business on the level and to give every man the opportunity to live in a free country.
Will the minister tell us when it is expected the commission will conclude its inquiries and be able to make a report?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I expect that they should conclude their inquiries some time before the end of August, and we would hope that the report would be available some time this fall.
They have finished in Toronto and Montreal? Are they now in the mari-times or going west?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are going west.

I am going to pass one remark. I am wondering whether I am really with "Alice" in "Wonderland". We have free enterprise parties all over the house and they are asking the government to interfere with free competition.

The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar said a little while ago-perhaps I will not say any more; it was a private conversation. I will say, however, that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar knows very well that the remark he has just made is not a proper interpretation of what is asked for here. I can tell the hon. gentleman if he really expects the house to be closed by Saturday he should refrain from making that sort of remark. I suggest that as a matter of fact what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would like to see, in keeping with the political doctrines to which he subscribes, is the continuance of conditions which would create a demand for government interference and control of everything. That would suit the purpose of the hon. gentleman.
We recognize that human nature has certain weaknesses and what we are trying to prevent are the abuses which will result from the kind of thing which the hon. gentleman wants continued. We maintain that these abuses are brought about under the system which is permitted as a result of the government legislation of 1951. The protection that had been worked out previously by business and commercial interests on a voluntary and co-operative basis was working well, as the
[Mr. Yuill.l
hon. member for Eglinton pointed out, in the interests of both the buyer and the seller. But it is now made illegal to follow that form of self-protection as a result of the ill-advised course followed by the government in 1951. We are not asking for any governmental protection for anyone. We are merely asking that those interested in the matter should be allowed to work out their own means of self-protection, a means which at the present time is made illegal by the government.

Could the minister tell us if there is any examination under way at the present time regarding some of the regulations in force in our penitentiaries? I fully realize that a person who breaks the law must pay the penalty and such persons must not be coddled. There is no question about that. But I do think the time has come for the revision of some of these regulations. I think they are a little bit too onerous. For example, I think an inmate of the penitentiary is allowed two letters per month. If a man is in a penitentiary for a considerable number of years it seems to me a little bit tough that he should be tied down to two letters a month, or three if he does not have any visitors for a period of four weeks. I have spoken to men in the penitentiary and they tell me they can send a letter to their wives, one to their mothers, and that is all. They cannot write their brothers, sisters, or others. I am wondering if there is any possibility of reconsidering regulations such as that and introducing some slight change for the better.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member must be clairvoyant because it so happens that that particular matter is under consideration at the present time.

The last time we had the
minister s estimates before us he had a report on this twelve-year-old boy who is serving a two-year sentence in St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. The hon. member for The Battle-fords suggested that there certainly must be two sides to this story. The minister promised to get a report from his officers. I wonder if he has that report available?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. I have it here somewhere. I undertook with my hon. friend from Mackenzie to get a report as to how this boy was getting along in the penitentiary. This is the report. I am not going to give his name, of course, or his number:
-has been transferred to the federal training centre on the 26th March, 1954, one day after his admission to St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. Because of his youth and need of sympathy and comprehension he was given special treatment. A scooter was provided,-

Supply-Justice
That sounds rather extraordinary but I think those members who saw him in the penitentiary will realize that it makes sense in an exceptional case like this to provide a scooter for an inmate of a penitentiary. The report continues:
-he was given small toy trucks, a meccano set etc., etc.-and as it is known that every boy wants to be the owner of a dog, he was given a young pup. -is segregated from the older and wiser inmates-he has a room, all by himself, in the hospital wing, where he has contacts with the hospital orderlies. Takes his meals in the chief steward's office under the supervision of a trustee-inmate-works at light duties-goes to school and does much physical exercises in the gymnasium under the coaching and guidance of the P.T. instructor. Seems to have adjusted fairly well to his new mode of living and no doubt is better off here than any other place he ever went-
Then it is noted here by the conscientious officer that it was only the scooter that was paid for at public expense. The other playthings were supplied by voluntary contributions from the officers.

This report supports the opinion that I expressed here. I think the content of the minister's report would indicate that the young lad is really quite a promising lad. I am sure that he is now having a better time than he ever had before. I wonder whether the minister sent along the report he placed on Hansard the last time he discussed the matter? Would he indicate whether he has sent that report along to the officers at the training school and has asked them to comment on that sort of report.
The point I am trying to get at is this. Here is a lad who, I think, should not have been in the penitentiary at any time in his life. The fact that he has had this preferred treatment from the officers at the federal training school would indicate that they think he has the makings of a citizen. But as I understood the situation before, he would be a problem of the provincial authorities and, if he gets a long enough sentence, he becomes a problem for the federal authorities. I think that the report that was placed on the record before was certainly a very one-sided report. I wish at the same time the minister would ask his officers to comment on the sort of report that he placed on the record.

On June 3, when the Department of Justice estimates were before the committee, I made a short statement on the problem of after-care of the discharged prisoners. I was glad to hear the minister say that recidivism has decreased to an encouraging extent since the new reform program was instituted. I just want to pursue the matter further at this time and to obtain some further details, if possible, as to how the problem of after-care is being met by the department.

First of all may I say this. Under this item 174 I notice that again there is $40,000 set aside for grants to recognized prisoners' aid societies as may be approved by the treasury board. I presume that that amount is divided among the three voluntary societies that were mentioned on June 3, namely the John Howard Society, the Elizabeth Fry Society and the Salvation Army. I wonder whether it is possible for the minister to indicate just what the percentage of distribution is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think perhaps my hon.
friend's previous remarks were confined to a local situation, and that it would perhaps be more accurate if I were to give the figures for the whole of Canada.
That is fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are as follows for 195354: The Canadian Penal Association, Toronto, $1,500; the Canadian Welfare Association, Winnipeg, $3,500; the Catholic Rehabilitation Service, Montreal, $500; the Elizabeth Fry Society, Kingston, $250; the John Howard Society at the following places: St. John's, Newfoundland, $500; Halifax, Nova Scotia, $2,000; Moncton, New Brunswick, $1,000; Saint John, New Brunswick, $500; Montreal, Quebec, $1,750; Toronto, Ontario, $7,750; Saskatoon, $1,000; Calgary, $3,000; Vancouver, $3,250; Victoria, $750; la Societe d'Orientation et de Rehabilitation, Montreal, $5,000; Salvation Army public service, Toronto, $2,000. That is a total of $35,000.

I wish to thank the minister for that information. As he has indicated in those figures, the support is widely distributed across the country. I think any money spent in this way is used to the best possible advantage because from any knowledge I have of the problem the only facilities available outside the penitentiary for carrying out a program of after-care are provided by these voluntary groups.
I have one further question in this regard. The minister indicated that in the case of these prisoners coming up for discharge a trained psychologist makes a thorough examination of the case. I presume that when he uses the word "psychologist" he indicates that there is just one person engaged for this activity for all the institutions in Canada.
I looked in the estimates and I note that there is a vote for one psychologist only. On this point, may I say that an employment circular was sent out from the remission service of the Department of Justice-it is competition number 54594, June 3, 1954-advertising for a clemency officer. I conclude that this is an addition to the staff and is in addition to

the psychologist who has already been referred to. Perhaps I had better complete my remarks on this topic while I am on my feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Might I answer these questions now? By doing so I will not overlook any of them.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The clemency officer is not an officer of the penitentiary service at all. He is attached to the remission service, and he investigates and advises upon the exercise of clemency in remission matters. As regards the psychologist, I think my hon. friend from Brandon-Souris will find if he will look at Hansard that what I said before was that we had a psychiatrist in nearly all of the penitentiaries, and that we had likewise in each penitentiary an official who is called a classification officer but who is a trained psychologist. It may be that my hon. friend has reference to another psychologist who will come on the staff under the name of psychologist, but all our classification officers are university graduates trained in psychology, and we have them in addition to our psychiatrists.

Perhaps I have misunderstood that point. I was looking specifically for psychologists and I could find a reference only to one. On the question of after-care, I am interested in the re-establishment credits that are available to prisoners. While voluntary organizations, particularly the Salvation Army, provide hostel facilities and so forth for the discharged prisoner, in the first few weeks following his discharge he is pretty largely dependent on any re-establishment credit he has built up during his stay in the institution. Has there been any increase in the per diem allowance within recent years? It was a very small sum. I should also like to know whether it is given in a lump sum or apportioned over a period of time so that the man will not, in the first flush of freedom, spend it on riotous living and get himself into further difficulty.
The same problem confronted the serviceman. There were various checks and balances on re-establishment credits so that the serviceman would make the best use of the money. In the case of a discharged prisoner the problem is of course all the greater. Finally, is it possible for the prisoner while he is in the institution to build up additional credits as the result of his work in the prison workshops and, if so, on what basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Every prisoner when he is discharged gets a suit of clothes and his transportation. Prior to 1951 prisoners were paid
Supply-Justice
-it was not by way of gift at all-a flat five cents per day for the work they did while in prison. They had the privilege of spending a small portion of that. As a matter of fact there was not too much on which to spend it and the bulk of it would be saved against release. We felt that this was a rather inadequate wage. At the present time, as the result of a change made in 1951, 15 per cent of the penitentiary inmates are being paid a wage of 20 cents per day, 45 per cent are being paid 15 cents per day and 40 per cent 10 cents per day. The great bulk of this accumulates and since it is the prisoner's own money we do not hold it back over a period of time after his release. We give him the whole amount when he is discharged.
I think I should add that he is discharged under an arrangement made before his discharge between the classification officer and the prisoners' aid society in charge of his case, such as the John Howard Society, the Salvation Army. The employment service of Canada also are interested in seeing to it that he can get employment. Therefore although he has not much money he has a pretty good chance to become re-established, particularly with the assistance he gets both from the penitentiary officials and these other re-establishment bodies.

Actually when a man comes out of a penitentiary he has not a great deal of money. I am told that the average is around $25. While in prison he has to spend money for tobacco and other things which he can buy at the commissariat in the penitentiary. Everything possible should be done to encourage these men to build up their own resources because if they come out of the penitentiary with a sufficient amount of money there is only a small chance that they will go back to a life of crime.
I feel there is one way in which the penitentiary officials can give greater encouragement, and I should like to commend it to the attention of the minister. In my estimation the penitentiary authorities are doing a magnificent job at the present time in the encouragement of hobbies. I know that in the British Columbia penitentiary the work, attitude and encouragement of the officials are excellent. The men are responding, and they are taking to hobbies in such a manner that some very skilled work is being done. Unfortunately, however, they are up against the problem of really making any money out of their hobbies on account of the lack of a market. I understand that in the past organized labour has always objected to anything manufactured in a penitentiary being sold on the open market, but I fail to see why organized labour should be afraid of the

Supply-Justice
marketing of the quantity of hobby goods that would come out of our penitentiaries.
I should like the minister to give consideration to giving greater assistance to inmates in the marketing of their hobby products. I think it would give them a great deal of encouragement. It would enable them to have more money at the time of their release and to a great extent might provide them with trades which they could enter on being released. I have been asked in the past few days where I got this wonderful tie I have been wearing. It is a hand-painted tie. I have been asked by members where they can buy one. It came from the British Columbia penitentiary. It is the hobby work of one of the inmates, a chap who is serving seven years. This is not the first time he has been in the penitentiary, but now he is doing this beautiful work. Inlay work, straw work and needlework are also being carried on and some marvellous things are being done.
I am certain that what are hobbies to these men at the present time can become trades or professions if they are given a little more assistance in the marketing of their products. I hope the minister, with all his other duties and responsibilities, will see if more attention cannot be given to overcoming the problem of the marketing of hobby products.

I believe that the work done in our penitentiaries extends far beyond hobbycrafts. The inmates engage in rather extensive furniture construction, shoe manufacturing and so forth. Can the minister tell us whether any of these products are disposed of to government departments? For example, public works uses considerable quantities of furniture and the armed forces use quite a number of shoes. If there is a problem in marketing these goods, as indicated by the hon. member for Vancouver East, it seems to me that might be a potential outlet. In my opinion the competition that might be provided by prison labour is greatly overexaggerated. I do not have the statistics, but I do not imagine that the total penitentiary population engaged in this type of activity would be more than 2,000. They do not work the full day because of the institutional schedule; they work only four hours a day five days a week. This would not represent a very formidable labour force, and yet it seems to me that they might find a ready market for their articles with some of the government departments. Just what is the situation in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I want to express my gratification at the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Vancouver East and

the hon. member for Brandon-Souris. One of the problems in providing genuine work for the inmates of the penitentiary, than which there is no greater rehabilitative agent -I mean real work and not just some make-work exercise that the prisoners do grudgingly-one of the great problems, I say, is public opinion which is opposed to having the production of prison labour come into competition with commercial articles. I am glad to have the members of the opposition express the views that they have expressed tonight.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris is quite right in saying, and I think his figures are approximately right too, that our prisoners form such a small proportion of the total working force of the nation that the competition of their product cannot be very alarming. Actually, however, this product is surprisingly good; our production has gone up from some $600,000 to over $1,200,000, although there is included in that a lot of the goods and services which are produced by the inmates of penitentiaries for their own use. As minister I am very glad to have this expression of opinion because we are considering the matter at this time and the suggestions made by hon. members are very apropos.
With regard to the sale of the hobbycrafts, the prisoners may send their products to relatives or they can sell them to the officers or visitors in the prison. From time to time special sales are arranged by service clubs or John Howard societies, where the sponsorship of an organization of that sort invites public interest and avoids public criticism.

In giving the list the minister started in with Kingston and gave the total number appointed as 30, 11 of whom were veterans. Could the minister give the same figures for the other institutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, certainly. St. Vincent de Paul, total 47; federal training centre, total 44; Dorchester, total 18; Manitoba, 18; British Columbia, 33; Saskatchewan, 19; Collin's Bay, 23; headquarters, 18.

I accept the minister's statement, Mr. Chairman, that the veterans preference is recognized. From these figures it is obvious that quite a number of veterans are being employed. I hope that every care is taken to see that that is the case, and at no institution are veterans applications not received. Would the minister have any knowledge of any instance of applications of veterans not being received and dealt with?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Absolutely not, sir.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I should like to make an
observation or two in connection with this item. I think we all appreciate very much the improvements that have been made in more recent times in so far as our penitentiaries are concerned, and more particularly the craftwork and the training of the inmates of the institution for useful occupations when
Supply-Justice
they go back into civilian life. In our own penitentiary in Manitoba, those of us who have had the privilege of visiting the institution recognize the very valuable groundwork of training that is being done there in fitting these people to take their part in life when they get out again.
I happen to have in my hand another little innovation which I thought indicated a very useful effort on the part of the institution. It is the publication of a little pamphlet in the form of a monthly news bulletin known as the Mountain Echo. It is a well prepared booklet having to do mostly with the institution, the life therein and some of the personnel. I look upon it as a creditable effort, and one in which those who are associated with the institution, particularly those within it, can take pride. The publication is in my opinion something that should be commended.
Then I understand an effort has been made recently to introduce sports to these institutions. From what I can gather, and from the contacts I have had with the institution in Manitoba, this innovation has played a very important part and is well accepted by those who are there. When outside teams and competitors take part in the games the results are good not only for the institution but for those from the outside, in that it gives an opportunity to see just what the rules of the game are, and it also gives the opportunity for the participants from outside and inside the institution to meet each other.
However I have risen more particularly at this time to ask the minister a question concerning the hours of labour guards who are associated with the institution are obliged to work. I realize the government introduced a 40-hour five-day week in many government services, but that it did not apply to the penitentiaries. It may well be that it is not possible to do all this at once. But I do submit to the minister-and I hope he will keep this in mind-that in my view guard duty at penitentiaries is one of the most hazardous, if one may so describe it, one of the most dangerous, and certainly one of the most nerve-straining occupations in which one could indulge. And if any branch of government service is to be recognized as being entitled to shorter hours of employment, then I suggest the guards and others in the penitentiaries are in that position.
I recognize immediately that a project of this kind would go beyond the guards. At the same time it would have to include personnel who are carrying on training, and things of that nature. At the same time I believe it would be admitted that, after all, the guards have the greatest measure of responsibility, and are perhaps under the

Supply-Justice
greatest strain of any group in the institutions. I would hope that early steps could be taken to place them in the same position as others in the government service, so that they may have the advantage of the shorter hours of employment, and that such a program might be worked out in the not too distant future. I wonder if the minister could indicate any plans directed to that end, or if he would tell us what is being considered in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend from Portage-Neepawa will recall that when the Minister of Finance announced the granting of the 40-hour week in the federal civil service he indicated at that time that there were some operating services in which it was not possible to introduce that provision. The penitentiaries form one of those operating services. One of the reasons as provincial governments have found is that, in institutions such as federal penitentiaries, provincial mental hospitals, provincial prisons and the like, up until the present time the difficulties of introducing the 40-hour week have proven to be insuperable, with the result that they have not been introduced in any of those institutions. I think it is likely that the introduction of the 40-hour week in our institutions would probably coincide with that in the corresponding provincial institutions.
Mr. Chairman, I have one further question.
Ah!

Somebody over there is in distress.
I note at page 227 that considerable sums are set aside for construction, improvements and new equipment in the penitentiaries. In that connection I presume that, as is indicated by the heading, the new equipment concerns the extension of training programs. When the minister replies I would appreciate it if in a general way, and without giving too much detail, he would indicate the purpose for which this money is being used. I would ask him particularly to tell us how much of the vote is distributed between technical training and vocational training.
Contacts I have had with this type of work going on in the penitentiaries indicate that there is a substantial percentage of money for penitentiary training being used for the training of machinists, and that the investment in machinery is high. It is pointed out however that the enrolment in that particular type of work is low in proportion to the amount of money invested in the machines.
In the institution I contacted the suggestion was put forward that perhaps the emphasis might be placed upon broader vocational training rather than training in a specialized category, and that the net results would be more beneficial. That is, it seems difficult to get a sufficient number of prisoners interested in strictly technical training as contrasted with other vocational opportunities. What is the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know where my hon. friend got the information that there is any difficulty in persuading prisoners to take, for example, machinists courses. I have been through the Collin's Bay vocational training school, and when I was there all these courses were up to their full complement. There were as many pupils as the instructors could handle. I believe that is typical. The equipment used in all the courses-plumbing, steamfitting, carpentry, masonry, machinists and the like-has been most effective in producing good results. I believe I am right in saying that the rate of recidivism is less than 15 per cent among those inmates who have taken these vocational training courses, and have subsequently been released from prison. This is a very low rate indeed when one considers that the percentage of recidivism among prisoners in the penitentiaries is up around 38 per cent in respect of previous penitentiary sentences and 77 per cent in respect of the service of previous terms in penitentiaries, reformatories or provincial jails sentences. Therefore, while this is a fairly large item of expenditure I think we get big dividends from it not only in the rehabilitation of prisoners but in the saving of future costs of maintaining them if they have to come back in prison again.
I do not want to press this matter too closely. Are there any statistics indicating the numbers involved in the various trades?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend will find it in the penitentiary report. If he has not one I will send him one.

Just on the subject of education, I want to say one word. I will not delay the committee. Two years ago I discussed this subject and asked for more complete information with regard to the education of those who are in our penitentiaries. I note that more complete information has been supplied. I thank the minister for that. I do not for one minute think that it came as a result of my discussion in the house. I note on page 177 the complete list of excellent tables. Would it not be much better to show the recidivists by the same system as is

shown elsewhere. On page 177 the recidivists are grouped under school grades 1 to 13 rather than putting them into the more normal division of elementary and high school. I suggest that that is a change for another year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be inclined to agree with my hon. friend, but those statistics are prepared by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Pass the word on to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Fine.

I want to ask a question by reading a sentence from page 12 which refers to overcrowding conditions. I understand that this has not been mentioned before:
Owing to the overcrowding conditions at these two institutions,-
The reference there was to St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary and Kingston penitentiary. -transfers were arranged to Dorchester and Manitoba penitentiaries where more accommodation was available.
Will the minister say a word as to overcrowding? It seems to me to be a serious matter. I should like to know whether this is further taken care of, or are arrangements in hand to take care of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The answer to the question that was asked a moment ago by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris is that these moneys were being spent largely for buildings, and this is also the answer to the question which my hon. friend has just asked. We are providing in these estimates that are under consideration fairly substantial sums of money to increase our accommodation for prisoners.
The fact of the matter is that our penitentiary population reached its low point in 1943, at which time it was slightly under
3,000	inmates. It stood fairly constant until about 1943, and from that time started to increase, and has increased pretty steadily year by year, until as of April 30 of the present year it went over the 5,000 mark. We have had to receive these inmates, and house and care for them.
Are these figures strictly comparable? Do they refer to exactly the same classes?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the total population of the penitentiaries, and that has presented a substantial problem because it is an increase of 66 per cent in a fairly short period. And that is one reason why we appreciate the suggestions of the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris about finding greater acceptance of the products of prison labour. We have not only to house those prisoners, we have to
Supply-Justice
keep them employed at some useful occupation. This heavy increase in penitentiary population has come about notwithstanding the fact that we have been able to improve the rate of recidivism of those inmates who are discharged from the penitentiary. Usually it is not our own graduate coming back upon us. We have been holding down our own rate of recidivism; but as the rate of recidivism from our institutions went down the rate of crime in society generally has been going up.
One of the purposes of our commission on remissions is to see if we cannot by some different system of parole, not only remission in the federal field but also parole in the provincial field, have a smaller number of inmates in our provincial prisons or federal prisons to take care of in proportion to the total number of prisoners convicted. On the American continent we have as compared with Britain and some of the European countries a quite high percentage of prisoners who upon being convicted are sentenced to imprisonment in our institutions. If we were able by a new system of parole or remission to cut that percentage down it would be one way of reducing the prison population both in our federal and in our provincial institutions. As matters have been up to the present time, we have just had to accept this increase in persons sentenced to imprisonment in federal penitentiaries. We have had very little control over this ourselves. We try to keep the factors over which we have control in order. It is the factors over which we have no control which are not in good shape. As a result we have to accept these prisoners and make provision for them.

Are they stationed at headquarters or included in the land, air, or marine services?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend is looking at but if he looks at the grand total of pay for the forces then that will include all the items we have stated, namely, headquarters administration, national police services, training establishments, land, air, and marine services, and civilian employees.

Then I will come to the reason for my question. I notice that under this first item, which puzzles me, details of which are given at page 474, there is an item listed for pay for members of the force amounting to $4,385,630. Then under item 409, details at page 476, there is an amount of $14,132,180 for pay for members of the force. My question was directed to the fact that the total pay for the headquarters staff members of the force is over one-quarter of the total for the land, air, and marine services. Therefore more than one-quarter of the pay of the members of the forces is devoted to the pay of those at headquarters. That is why I asked for the breakdown because it occurred to me to ask whether that is not a rather high proportion of the total personnel of the force. It appears there is approximately one-quarter of the total force stationed at headquarters. I realize my comment might have to be modified and that this apparently includes the training establishment. That is why I would like to be certain that the figure of 540 is inclusive of all the recruits who are undergoing training and does not merely indicate administrative personnel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend has this breakdown before him but the total to which he refers does include 425 constables who are undergoing training. Now does this training establishment, whose strength has now been given as a total of 540, include those at the training establishment here in Ottawa, or does it cover whatever other training establishments there may be elsewhere? I understand there is a training establishment at Regina. Would that be carried on headquarters strength?

All attributed for this purpose to headquarters?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

What about recruits? Would they be included in the total for the purposes of pay?

One other matter in this regard which is common to the detail in all three of the main divisions deals with headquarters, and land, air, and marine services. I am wondering whether the increases in rates of pay which have been provided or are in contemplation are, in fact, confined to the civilian personnel?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As my hon. friend will recall from time to time during the period he has served here in the House of Commons there have been increases in the rates of pay of the members of the force; I refer to the actual constables, officers and so forth of the force. The increases applicable to officers and members of the force are so provided, whereas these civilian employees come under the civil service rates and have to be set up separately.
