speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. I think I have that here, Mr. Chairman. As my hon. friend will recall, the question he asked is set out at page 5486 of Hansard. I do not think it is necessary for me to read that question into the record again. The report that I have with regard to that matter is as follows. It takes the form of a letter dated June 14, 1954, from deputy commissioner J. D. Bird to myself relative to the question which my hon. friend asked. It reads as follows:
Re: Theft of stores from Department of National Defence (Army)-Camp Ipperwash, Ontario
The news clipping from the Free Press,-
I suppose that would be the London Free Press.
-dated April 30, 1954, and the page from Hansard of June 3, 1954, forwarded with your memorandum of 7-6-54, are returned herewith.
A review of all reports on file at this headquarters which deal with this investigation, has been made. There is no indication that a civilian was stopped on a street to effect seizure of any article. The news clipping indicates that a Thed-ford man was stopped on the street and his shoes removed. We have no report of such an incident having taken place. Further, reports do state that on two occasions, civilians were found to be in possession of army footwear and, as they had no other shoes, the civilians were allowed to retain them until they were able to purchase others and then hand over the army boots to our investigator.
This investigation is being conducted to ascertain whether or not infractions of the pertinent sections of the Criminal Code of Canada have been contravened (sections 433 and 439) and, in some cases, exhibits have been handed over voluntarily and, in others, were seized under the authority of a search warrant. We have no record of any case where one of these procedures was not followed.
That is to say, they were either handed over voluntarily-which would be quite lawful-or they were seized under the authority of a search warrant, as I correctly surmised when my hon. friend asked the question the other day. Hence there is no impropriety of any kind.
I thank the minister.

I realize that the minister would like to finish these estimates tonight, Mr. Chairman. I am wondering whether he would rather go on with the other items and let me say what I have to say later on or whether he would rather let me say what I have to say now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no preference, Mr. Chairman. If there are no other points that any of the other hon. members wish to raise, perhaps my hon. friend might make his remarks now.

I have one or two items I want to ask about later on.

Supply-J ustice

The minister was in the house this morning when I began asking the Prime Minister concerning his preparations to meet communism. My own feeling is that, as a nation and as individuals, we are not taking communism nearly seriously enough and that we are not taking anything like the measures we ought to take to cope with it. That is why I asked the Prime Minister those questions this morning. I think probably it might be well just to review those questions briefly so that we shall have them in our minds as I begin asking the questions I desire to ask.
I asked the Prime Minister first of all whether he intended to win the cold war. He implied that he intended to do so all right, but he did not say it as though he meant it very much, as far as I was concerned. This being so, what has he done in that respect, since last August 10, designed to win the cold war? The Prime Minister did not get around to answering that question at all. I should like to know what the Minister of Justice would say with respect to that matter. If I conceive the matter aright, the minister is the custodian of the internal security of Canada just as the Minister of National Defence is the custodian of the external security of Canada. If the minister disagrees with my conclusions in any of these respects, he might tell me so. Is that not a satisfactory way of putting it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes sir.

Then we shall proceed on that basis. If that is the case, one would naturally conclude that the Minister of Justice would have charge of moves made to offset the attack of communism. In other words, in the cold war he would not be remaining just on the defensive. He would be counterattacking and he would be able to give us the measures which he had used in the counter-attack. He would also be able to give us some idea concerning the success or the lack of success of his attack. I may be all wrong, Mr. Chairman, but I have not been able to find a single measure on the part of Canada that could by any stretch of the imagination be looked upon as a Canadian attack. We just seem to be sitting here in Canada like a lot of sitting ducks and to be letting the communists blaze away at us with all their methods of propaganda, shedding the shot as best we can and hoping that we shall be able to survive the last one. That is just the impression that Canada gives me.
I hope I am wrong but I am afraid I am right. I should like to open up that whole matter and to have the minister talk frankly to us as he likes to do. I admire the way the minister talks frankly to us and takes us 
into his confidence. I should like to hear from him. I am really anxious about this whole thing.
I asked whether the Prime Minister had had brought to his attention the communist over-all plan. The communists never stop. They have never stopped since 1917. In fact, the people who built up communism before 1917 were at work for many generations before that time. They never miss a trick. They never lose a play. They never stop. Long before they have won one victory, they know what the next victories are going to be and where they are going to strike. For example, I point to Guatemala. I imagine that they had the taking over of Guatemala all planned five years ago. I just hope that they are not planning on taking over British Columbia next. Certainly they have the stage all set for British Columbia next. That is just how close danger could be to us, I am afraid. Of course, I am not reflecting on the vigilance of the people in charge of British Columbia.
But later in the course of my remarks I probably will refer to a rather alarming article which appeared in the Financial Post of December 12, 1953. I think I will send it to the minister. Has he seen it? Then I take it he knows what is in the article. It certainly spoils a person's sleep for several weeks to contemplate that. That article says that there are 90,000 communists in British Columbia, and they are probably all ready to march. The writer of the article says 90,000, and in a general way I think he is not a man who should be disregarded.
Therefore I am afraid the Prime Minister would have to say that he had not done a single thing since August 10 to meet this situation. He did not know anything about the communist over-all world plan and he had not done anything to meet the offensive which is coming into Canada constantly from communist countries in the form of a cold war. I asked the Prime Minister also what specific measures he has taken to offset communism in Canada. How much does he know about the state of affairs in Canada?
I asked him particularly about three matters. What has he done to find out what are the techniques that communism has employed; what is the degree of success that communism has attained in Canada, and what are the possible means available to Canada to combat communism in Canada?
I am afraid the answer to every one of these three would be just plain nothing. If that is the case, then probably the responsibility rests on the minister.
If at any time he wishes to put me right as I go along I will welcome his speaking

because I have no desire at all to misrepresent the situation as it is. I have all respect for the minister. Then I asked: Does the Prime Minister know specifically what is the communist line in America for 1954? I pointed out that if a person knew what their line is in 1954 he would be able to tell when anyone spoke supporting that line. If anyone should speak supporting that line we would say at once, "That fellow is a communist, he will bear watching".
I asked the Prime Minister if he knew what the communist line was in 1953. There has been a change. They change their line every once in a while just like skilful players of chess, checkers or any other game. As a matter of fact, the communist high command just plays across the world like a skilful performer playing the piano. It just has us so completely dazzled, so completely bewildered that we do not even know what is going on. All we know is that something is happening to us but we have not the slightest idea what is causing it or how it is being produced. In many cases we blunder right into their line and help them just like a person playing checkers who jumps his own man. That is my general impression with respect to this matter.
I wanted to give the Prime Minister an idea of the sort of thing with which he is confronted here in Canada. I offered to read a passage from a broadcast in May and to comment on that broadcast. I want to be perfectly fair in every way both to Canada and to the man concerned. The other day I asked the question:	Who selected J. B.
McGeachy to be on the Speakers' list of the C.B.C.? There are several reasons why I asked that question. As hon. members will recall, I did not accuse Mr. McGeachy of being a communist. I did not accuse him of being disloyal. Some people try to make out that I did but I did not. But I was concerned. Let me read a short passage from his broadcast of May 9 as it was monitored to me. There may be errors in these words but I think they are accurate. Those who got them got them pretty accurately. He is talking about the Indo-China situation at a time when we were all greatly concerned about Indo-China and wondering if there was not something we could do to stop the progress of the Chinese communists, representing the Russian communists, into Indo-China. Here is what he told the Canadian people:
But without going in for prophecy, I will venture these opinions: First, that the best result to be hoped for in Indo-China is an armistice, followed by some compromise arrangement which, if possible, will give the Indo-Chinese a chance to decide what form of government they prefer; and second, that the west must come somehow to terms with, and live with, the Asian social revolution-
Supply-Justice
Notice the words, "social revolution", which it is not.
-whether it takes a communist form or. as in India, Pakistan and elsewhere, a non-communist form. No amount of military force exercised by the west will decide, from this day forward, the destiny of any Asian state.
May I tell the house how that affects me. In the first place, we were hoping to contain communism. I do not think there is anyone in the house who relishes seeing China extend her control to all of southeast Asia, including India, Pakistan and Burma, and then to Japan, Malaya and the Philippines. Is there any person in this country who would contemplate a prospect like that with equanimity? Is that not exactly what this man is suggesting?

On a point of order, as I understand it we are dealing with the estimates of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As far as I know their jurisdiction does not extend to southeast Asia, and it seems to me-

I did not get the last
words.

The jurisdiction and responsibility of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police do not extend to southeast Asia. If we are to finish these estimates tonight, I suggest that we stick to the point. Not only is the hon. member out of order but he has made some highly improper aspersions against a very reputable journalist by the name of McGeachy who is a person known to many members of the house, and such aspersions are resented.
I hope the hon. member, being a new member, learns better how to interpret what a man says than he has during this session. I have made no aspersions against this gentleman.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. A point of order having been raised at this time, I think perhaps I should indicate my reaction to the point of order of the hon. member for St. Paul's. The remarks of the hon. member for Lethbridge have been causing me some worry because I did not want to interrupt him. I believe that it is my duty as chairman not to seek ways and means of ruling a member out of order but to so interpret the rules of the house that he is not hampered in what he has to say. However, it is perfectly correct that the item before the house is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
It is my understanding that the physical combating of communism in Canada is in the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted

Supp ly-J ustice
Police. Therefore the hon. member for Lethbridge is entirely within his rights in discussing the combating of communism in Canada. I cannot help but agree that so far as we are aware the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have nothing to do with the combating of communism outside of Canada. Therefore when the hon. member for Lethbridge gets into countries far afield he might perhaps be in order under the Department of External Affairs but I cannot agree that he is in order under an item dealing with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
I think that the members of the committee are anxious to give the hon. member for Lethbridge a chance to say what he wishes to say in connection with the problem in Canada. If the hon. member will confine his remarks to Canada, I will do what I can to ensure that he proceeds uninterrupted.
Mr. Chairman, you have established a most enviable record for fairness in the past, and I am sure you will do the same tonight.

Would the hon. member permit a question, Mr. Chairman, which I think will clear up the whole matter. I may have misunderstood the hon. member, and I am glad to accept his statement, if I understand it correctly, that he does not cast any reflection on Mr. McGeachy in what he is saying tonight.

I made that clear. How many times does a person have to say that in good plain English before it registers?
I believe you were not in the chair, Mr. Chairman, or perhaps not in the chamber when I raised this matter this morning when the estimates of the Minister of Justice were opened. It was understood at that time I would be discussing the cold war, the whole struggle of the cold war and not necessarily in its relation to the way the mounted police would exercise their function in the country, so that would give me considerable latitude in order to reach out and deal with the communist question as a whole.
Now, it was to clear myself for that kind of attack that I pointed out to the minister, at the outset of my remarks, that as I thought the Minister of National Defence was responsible for the external security of Canada, the Minister of Justice was responsible for the internal security. May I now proceed to discuss the cold war? I believe that everyone will recognize that when Indo-China was attacked it strengthened the hands of communists in Canada and weakened the hands of those opposed to communism. Every one of these moves that I have indicated, the fall of the rest
[The Deputy Chairman.]
of eastern Asia, the fall of Japan, the fall of Korea, would certainly be steps in the cold war that would win victories over the people of the United States and of Canada.
I believe that with these considerations I am quite in order in the way I am proceeding. I would be glad to hear if the minister thinks I am not, but I cannot see how one could deal with communism and the cold war without looking upon it in a global way. After all, every move that they make is designed to accomplish a certain objective. If I, in your judgment, Mr. Chairman, begin to err as I go forward then I wish you would call my attention to the fact. I have no desire to do that, but I do have a desire to meet this problem of communism as a responsible member of the Canadian House of Commons in this fateful year of 1954 ought to do, having in mind that there are 15 million people in Canada who are dependent for their security upon us. I do not want to see a Guatemala in Canada or in any part of Canada.
Now, if I may proceed, I shall deal with the question of Mr. McGeachy's speech. I should be glad if the hon. member who raised the question would follow now, and if I seem to be casting any aspersions on this hon. gentleman I shall be glad to hear it and to modify my remarks. I have no desire to hurt anybody. My opinion is that Mr. McGeachy had no intention whatever of following the communist line in this speech, but I believe he was following the communist line in this speech. This is what I gather from this speech. His statement from, "without making any prophecy . . ." down to ". . . any Asian state", constituted an announcement to Russia and China that the green light is turned on. They are free to go ahead and conquer Japan, Malaya or the Philippines because we cannot stop them, and we have to learn to get along with all these people if they rebel under the direction, and with the assistance, of China.
In so far as Syngman Rhee and Chiang Kai-shek are concerned we are abandoning the freedom of their peoples by announcing there is no hope. To the United States it was an announcement that she should stand alone. If she wants to go over there and stop the Chinese, well and good; it is her lookout and we are not having anything to do with it. To all freedom-loving people in southeast Asia, and there are plenty of them who took part in the struggle in IndoChina, it amounted to this: you better make terms, boys, because you are going to be under the communists anyhow and there is no use getting them angry. To all the people of Canada it amounted to saying it is very

little concern of ours. To communists everywhere it amounted to saying: full steam ahead, boys; the sun is shining, so make hay.
Moreover, all through this passage ran two implied falsehoods. I am not saying that Mr. McGeachy intended them to be falsehoods but I am going to point them out and let hon. members draw their own conclusions as to how he should have made these two mistakes. He implied quite clearly that communism is a revolution. Communism never has been a revolution. From the beginning it has been a conquest by a conspiracy of men who went from the United States in large measure, were financed from the United States, and went across to Russia and beat down the Russian government. They established control and extended their control over Russia and from Russia to where we see them now. To call such a movement as that a revolution is to misuse the word "revolution".
The second error was even to suggest that communism may ever be satisfied with less than world conquest. We have made some terrible mistakes as American people since 1945 because we persisted in believing that somehow, somewhere we could get Russians to be satisfied, sit down and live peacefully. They have no thought of doing that. They take every move as a beachhead from which to make another move. They have told us over and over again that they intend to conquer the world. Why could a man like Mr. McGeachy make two such blunders as that, and why would the C.B.C. employ a man who would make blunders like that? You have these two blunders going to the people all over Canada and down into the United States as far as his voice would carry. I believe that is altogether different from the way it ought to be.
Perhaps I should give some evidence against the idea that communism is a revolution. May I read this very small excerpt from the economic council's letter in the United States dated April 1, 1954, letter No. 332. I read these words:
The U.S.S.R. is not a world power In the sense we have always thought-a government naturally looking out for its own interests but maintaining certain general standards of honour and integrity in international dealings. Rather, this Soviet government is nothing else than a gang of plotters who succeeded in the confused days of 1917 in making itself master of Petrograd formerly St. Petersburg, now Leningrad and extending that mastery to all of Russia.
May I interrupt now to ask if there is any hon. member in the house who can offer any reason why that statement is not absolutely correct? It is entirely in accordance with all the evidence that has come
Supply-Justice
down to us right from the time that the United States conducted their most searching inquiry into communism in 1919, when they were so close to the event they could name all the people who took part.
The next paragraph reads this way:
And now with the astounding assistance of the United States, it controls most of the Eurasian continent. It threatens to take over all southeast Asia, Japan, the Middle East, Italy, even France. It has a third of Germany under its inhuman control. There is not a country in the world, including the United States, that is not threatened with subjugation.
I do not think anyone would seriously question the accuracy of that statement. The people who prepared this letter are generally very careful, scholarly and reliable in what they say. And as I said, the information I have concerning the whole communist conspiracy bears out exactly what they say. In the light of that I ask whether J. B. McGeachy was following the communist line. He was saying just exactly what Russia would like him to say. He was giving comfort to the enemy, and in great volume. He was saying what every communist in the world would like him to say. And he was demoralizing every person opposed to communism who heard him, and making us feel unhappy.
Now, that is just one simple little illustration of the cold war, and the methods which Russia is using. People say: "What! Do you say Mr. McGeachy was an agent of Russia?" Oh, I would hate to say that, but there may be men in Canada with a good deal of power who have much more sympathy with Russia than they have with Canada, and those men could have had a lot of influence in getting that man put on the C.B.C. list of speakers. That is as far as I will go in that respect.
Then, before I finish what I have to say tonight, I wish to place on record a statement which apparently is authentic and which shows what the plans of the Chinese and the Russians are, right from here to 20 years from today, when they are confident that they will be ruling the world, including us. But I will come to that after a while.
Oh, do it now.

I will ask the minister if he agrees that we are in a fight to the finish against the communist conspiracy that rules Russia. I do not believe the minister will say under the circumstances that we are not. Very well, if we are in a fight to the finish, we are spending $2 billion a year preparing our army to go and fight. I said to the Minister of National Defence the other day that it was just simply idle to spend all this money, in preparing the army if we are going

Supply-J ustice
to allow ourselves to be beaten through the back door and the basement window. And that is exactly what we are doing when we turn a man like J. B. McGeachy loose on this country, through the C.B.C. Speeches like this-and certainly he has given others though perhaps not as bad as this-but a speech like this I think everyone will agree should not be allowed; and it will be agreed that I have not put an unfair interpretation upon it, especially as it was delivered on May 9.
And now may I read a statement coming from an exceedingly valuable book. I hope the minister has read it, but as he is a very busy man perhaps he has not had time to read it. I hope he will have a very dependable man in his department read the book and study it with the utmost care. I refer to "The Iron Curtain Over America" by Dr. John Beaty, published in 1952. I imagine this book is the most pertinent one bearing on what we are talking about tonight. Dr. Beaty says this in his introduction:
Only an informed American people can save America, and they can save it only if all those to whom it is given to know will share their knowledge with others.
That is all I am trying to do tonight, to share the little knowledge I have with others. This book, by the way, was published in 1952 and Dr. John Beaty is one of the finest scholars to be found anywhere in the world on this particular subject. He is an American who has had a most impressive career.
Now may I give an outline of the communist aims, as they are contained in a document which was read into the Congressional Record by Senator Knowland quite recently. He is not sure this is authentic, but it bears all the evidence of being authentic, and would appear to be the work of Chou En-lai, who is one of the master minds of China, and one of the master minds of the world today. This statement, by the way, is to be found at page 2 of the Ottawa Journal of June 1, where hon. members may read it if they wish. These are the steps Chou En-lai, or whoever wrote this document, says will be followed:
1.	We will avoid war until victory is certain.
How long will we have to avoid war before
victory is certain if China goes on and takes over all of Asia, including Japan with her 87 million people and her wonderful productive potential?
2.	Isolate the United States by all possible means.
3.	Britain must be placated by (a) the possibility of settling major issues,-

And that is what is troubling them today- the possibility of getting these people to be satisfied.
- (b) opportunities for trade, which Britain sorely needs.
Britain is not like us, possessed of rich resources. She has to trade to live. If we will not trade with her, she must trade with the east. And the sooner we understand that in America, the better.
4.	France has to be influenced by war-weariness and fear of Germany.
France is going that way right now, isn't she?
5.	We will liberate Indo-China.
6.	We will liberate Burma next.
As though Burma needed liberating!
7.	We will liberate Thailand next.
8.	The whole of Indonesia will be in the hands of communists by 1960.
In the light of the progress they have been making recently, that does not look extravagant, does it?
9.	Japan will capitulate after peaceful revolution backed by force by China and the Soviet union.
All we have to do is bear in mind the very serious difficulty Japan has with her 87 million in those restricted islands, with the small empire she once had now taken away from her, the extreme difficulty she has in securing the means to live. All we have to do is keep those conditions in mind with respect to Japan, and we will see what must almost certainly happen to her.
10.	If war can be averted the success of our plans for other parts of Asia is almost assured. This task will be completed in 1965.
11.	Then would follow a wave of revolution throughout Africa.
We do not put that beyond the realm of possibility, do we?
12.	Total economic collapse in capitalistic western Europe would follow as soon as Asia and Africa are disconnected from western Europe.
They would have no place to sell their goods, nowhere to buy from, and being capitalist, they would think they could not live. Then western Europe will capitulate and fall to communism.
13.	With the fall of western Europe, remaining capitalist countries will face economic collapse and industrial breakdowns.
That may sound extreme until one looks at the pathetic spectacle that Canada and the United States are making right now in respect of wheat. Because we cannot sell wheat abroad, we fear we cannot live! We bring down the price of our wheat. We begin to create a price cutting panic. We would simply have to sell abroad! If we could not

we would have to sit down, droop our shoulders and cry because we could not sell it.

What has the R.C.M.P. to do
with that?
The point is that if we cannot manage our affairs better than that, we should be able to. And surely the hon. member, who has been a member of a legislature-

the same hopeless and defenceless condition. Twenty years from now, that Chinese statesman says, the world revolution will be an accomplished fact.
I shall take the hon. member's question if he would like to ask it.

It is not for me to defend the mounted police. The minister is much more capable of doing that than I am. This is my question. Has the hon. member had any dealings with the mounted police in regard to communist activities?

Of course I do not see
just what bearing that has on the point I am dealing with now.

If the hon. member has any information to give to the mounted police he has only to do as I have done at different times and he would find them to be most co-operative and in fact ready to act at any time. I can relate one circumstance where the parish priest in my riding-at that time I was a member of the provincial house- was very much worried about the activities of one man in his parish, a newcomer in fact. I met the mounted policeman who was at that time stationed at Timmins. 1 asked him to stop on his way back at that place and see the parish priest. He had no sooner walked into the parish priest's house than he was greeted by the parish priest and he said: "Most likely, Reverend Father, you are going to ask me about Mr. So and So." The parish priest was really surprised. He said: "Yes, that is exactly the case." The policeman said: "You need not worry; we know all the facts about that man; we are following every move he makes." I can tell the hon. member it would be far better for him to give any information he has to the mounted police. By so doing he would certainly serve his country better than to try to start in this country what other countries have tried to do by throwing smears on everybody in the country.

In the first place, "the member" did not try to throw a smear at anyone, and I challenge the hon. member to show that I did. I am telling the absolute truth, not smearing anyone. If the facts are smearing a man, it is his own fault.
The next point is this, if the mounted police are as magnificent a force as the hon. member believes they are, and I believe they are too, why not give them the ghost of a chance and not have propaganda coming in here making their work many times more difficult? Surely, there is a limit to the endurance of any force of men! I am merely pointing out the terrible dangers that confront us, and which will probably run right on

Supply-Justice
if we do nothing to offset them. The hon. member will be lost before he will realize what is happening.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
First of all, I want to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Lethbridge for the very very kind and rather unusual action on his part in allowing me to interrupt his remarks to answer the questions which he has asked. As the hon. member has correctly stated, the responsibility of the special branch of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and of myself as the minister in charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is the internal precautions against communism in Canada. Those internal precautions have already been the subject of reference in the debate on the justice estimates previously this session. I made a statement then in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East, which I should like to repeat now because I think what I said then is precisely relevant to the points which the hon. member for Lethbridge has been raising this evening.
As I understand the hon. member he wants to get an answer to these questions. He asked:
What specific measure has the Prime Minister- and in that connotation I include the Prime Minister, the government and the mounted police- taken to offset communism in Canada?
(a)	In discovering what techniques communism is employing?
(b)	What is the degree of success communism has obtained in Canada?
(c)	What are the possible means available to Canada of combating communism in Canada?
I pointed out when this matter was before the committee previously that what we were discussing in questions like these was the practice of espionage and counter-espionage, and I said that I was sure hon. members upon the least reflection would agree that it would be a grave error indeed to discuss here any of the activities of the special branch of the mounted police and especially to admit or deny any allegations of sometimes irresponsible people claiming to have been in our employ in counter-espionage. I said, and I now quote directly from Hansard at page 5464:
We are all aware that the practice of espionage and counter-espionage, the contest between enemy nations to secure and to prevent the securing of intelligence involves the building up, as completely as possible, of a large mass of information; and oftentimes the answer in the affirmative or negative to some simple statement of fact may be the last item needed to complete the general pattern of, if I may use that figure of speech, the jigsaw puzzle which the intelligence department is trying to put together; and this last simple answer may finally determine what that whole pattern is.
In counter-espionage work there is therefore only one safe policy to follow, and that is the policy of complete reticence about our counter-espionage and complete reticence in respect of the espionage against which we are trying to protect Canada. It

is for that reason that we have consistently refused to say anything with regard to the allegations of gentlemen like-
A certain gentleman whom I then named; and it is for that reason, Mr. Chairman, that I am sure my hon. friend, the hon. member for Lethbridge, would be the last man in this house to take any action or to ask any questions the answers to which would give any aid or comfort to the communists whether inside or outside of Canada. I pay him that tribute.
But I think the hon. member himself will agree upon reflection that if we were to discuss in this house the techniques which communism is employing, and made disclosures as frank as those disclosures I like to make in relation to other branches of the Department of Justice, there is nothing in the world that would be more helpful to the communists than to know precisely how much we do know about them and therefore by inference what we do not know. No one would be more happy to have this information than the communists themselves.
In the same way, if we were to indicate the opinion of our experts in the special branch as to the degree of success communism has attained in Canada-and we think we know something about this matter-then that information disclosed in this house would be carried thence in the press of the world. What action could we take which would help the communists more than that?
If I were to answer the third question as to what other possible means are available in Canada for combating communism in Canada I would be giving away our whole program of counter-espionage and by that means largely destroying its usefulness. It is for that reason and that reason only that I must reluctantly refuse to answer the questions my hon. friend from Lethbridge has asked. Even after what I said the other day in this debate upon the Department of Justice estimates in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East, I have not reached that conclusion nor did I reach that conclusion with regard to the specific questions asked by my hon. friend, until I had again conferred, after my hon. friend has asked questions of the Prime Minister, with the high officials of the special branch of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. This is the opinion which they expressed with regard to the specific questions asked by the hon. member for Lethbridge:
Upon a study of (a), (b), and (c) -
These were the three branches of my hon. friend's question.
-it becomes very apparent that they are allembracing and if answered would supply intelligence to not only communists themselves but to

foreign powers, and as we know that both the communists and certain foreign powers are continually attempting to procure this type of information,-
And may I say, Mr. Chairman, that I think pretty largely unsuccessfully.
-we deem it most inadvisable to supply this to them, in even the barest detail. It is, therefore, suggested that the question be answered along the following lines:
And they suggested the type of answer which I am now giving. I must say, Mr. Chairman, I have always admired the frankness and candour of the hon. member for Lethbridge and I am temperamentally disposed to be frank and candid myself. I would have very much preferred to have given him a detailed answer on all these questions but I am sure he will agree upon reflection that to do so would certainly not be in the best interests of Canada.
Now, if I may, while I am on my feet, I think I should discharge an act of friendship to a gentleman whose name has come into this discussion. The gentleman to whom I refer is Mr. J. E. McGeachy. I have known him for many years. Indeed, I know him better than I know the hon. member for Lethbridge and I have known the hon. member for quite some time. I knew Mr. McGeachy when he was a reporter and editorial writer on the Winnipeg Free Press back in the 1930's. He afterwards became a very distinguished member of the staff of the British Broadcasting Corporation and on his return to Canada he has had an equally distinguished journalistic and broadcasting career here. One does not have to agree with all of his utterances to be sure that those who know him as I do would agree that he is not disposed to favour communism. As one who knows Mr. McGeachy I can say that whatever my hon. friend may say about his views, Mr. McGeachy is certainly not a communist by any stretch of the imagination. He is a good, loyal, intelligent Canadian and while my hon. friend from Lethbridge may not agree with all of his opinions I do not think that that warrants any accusation of him being in any way disposed to favour the communists or communism.

I hope the hon. member for Lethbridge will not mind if I say a few words at this juncture. I do not want to interrupt the continuity of anything he might wish to say, but I would like to say briefly that I listened with a good deal of interest to the minister's reply and I would sum it up by saying that the minister seems particularly responsible for matters that might be stressed in terms of physical sabotage, and that the R.C.M.P. is certainly doing a 83276-416i
Supply-Justice
good job in preparing information and warning the government of what is going on particularly in a physical sense. Perhaps they know everything that is happening within those organizations in which communist card holders may be at work. They are ready to pick up anyone who may sabotage a piece of machinery, or something of that kind. But it seems that some of us are not quite satisfied with government action in another field of sabotage and that is in the sabotaging of our minds and our moral standards, and action in helping to prepare the people to withstand the onslaught of communist propaganda which might come from innocent sources.
The name of a certain reporter has been brought into the discussion. Fortunately or unfortunately it may be a matter of interpretation, and it is true that the discussion could have taken place without any names being brought into the picture. But just as sure as I was born if the hon. member for Lethbridge had read some extract from a speech given over the air someone would be bound to rise and ask who gave the speech, so there is little difference. It might come from an innocent source but the fact remains that there is a process of conditioning going on, a conditioning of the mentality of our Canadian people to accept the enemy as they attempt to come in by the back door, and some of us are not satisfied that the government is taking appropriate steps in that respect. That is something you cannot handcuff. You cannot handcuff an idea. The only way you can meet it is with a counteridea and we are not satisfied that that is being done.
The minister could have answered on behalf of the mounted police along the lines I have indicated. We are all free to say we believe they are doing a good job, but it is this other angle about which we have so much concern. You can have sabotage by the back door method just as easily as you can have it by the blowing up of a few factories, and more so. That is where the greater danger may lie in this whole thing.
I hope the hon. member for Lethbridge will excuse me for just butting in at this particular point.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Macleod has made it unnecessary for me to answer the minister. I think he has done an admirable job. He has put the situation in just exactly the way it needs to be put. I will just refer to the question of Mr. McGeachy since he has been mentioned. I am sure all that I have heard about him indicates that the estimate made by the

Minister of Justice is exactly right concerning him. I am satisfied that he is an admirable gentleman, although I have never met him. I hope to meet him some day and to have him as a good friend.
I would say this to the minister. In the first place, if there are speakers like Mr. McGeachy who are following the communist line, maybe unwittingly, over the radio, surely the government should know enough about what the communist line is to be able to detect all these speeches which are along the communist line and cause them to be modified; or if it is deemed wise that such speeches should be given, why not have speeches too that will answer them?
Who will censor them?

We can easily find people to censor them. I am sure the hon. member can ask questions which are much more worth while than that if he tried to do so.
What I have said concerning this passage from Mr. McGeachy's speech I believe will istand up flawlessly under the interpretation which I have placed on it. There will be no answer to what I have said. Coming as it did, it was comfort to the enemy in every respect. That speech could have been answered by another speech by some other gentleman putting forward the other point of view. That is a measure that the minister might have mentioned, but did not mention.
I thank the minister very much for the interpolation. I think I will now follow on and give some other considerations which I believe to be of tremendous importance at this time in Canada. Certain it is that regardless of all that we may say we are losing the cold war. I think there is not a responsible member in this chamber who will not agree that we are losing the cold war.
That is comfort to the enemy.

That is true. It is comfort to the enemy. But we may just as well confess it and then try to do something about it.
The next thing is this. We won world war II. We poured out blood and treasure. We won it. But certain people inside the administrations of the nations that won the war threw China into the hands of the enemy and put the whole body of freedom-loving nations in a position where it is doubtful that we shall be able to survive. That is a terrible thing. For us to contribute to that process any further borders on simple foolhardiness. We simply must do something to change all that.

May I now go on commenting to some extent on certain other aspects of this question as I see them. There are three main aspects of the fight against communism. In the first place, we have to deal with spying. Then we have to deal with sabotage. Then we have to deal with propaganda which influences public opinion and shapes our policies. I think the hon. member for MacLeod did fairly well with regard to the subject of sabotage and its danger.
As far as spying is concerned, may I say that although the minister thinks that Russia does not know our secrets, I doubt whether we have in Canada a secret that Russia does not know better than we know it. When ministers of the government tell us that they do not want to let us have information because the enemy will get it, I often think that about the only people in the country who do not know it are the Canadian people generally and the members of the House of Commons. All the Russians and Chinese will know our secrets. That is what they have done with regard to United States secrets and that is what they are doing with ours-make no mistake about that-because they had already done it in 1945 and 1946 when Gouzenko came out and made the surprising revelations he made to us. As far as spying to obtain secrets is concerned, I have dealt with that matter. As to sabotage, it is extremely dangerous. Those 90,000 people in British Columbia are cause for genuine concern.
The minister feels that the mounted police are able to deal with them. Individually, man for man, I would say that the mounted police are as capable of dealing with a situation like that as are any force of men on the face of this earth. But I believe that it is well that we should look across the fence and see what is happening in the next yard. Here is something that J. Edgar Hoover told the United States subcommittee on appropriations on December 9,	1953,
regarding the 1955 appropriation request for the federal bureau of investigation. From page 163 may I quote a paragraph:
The investigative burden in covering the communist underground has been increased tremendously as is shown by the tact that where one agent was formerly needed for proper coverage, we now require as many as 9 or 10 by reason of their greater security consciousness in carrying out their conspirational activities. We have to change our surveillances more frequently by reason of their shifting of party members.
This report goes on through several pages giving material concerning difficulties being encountered down there in the United States

because the communists have gone underground. They have stopped carrying communist cards. They have stopped using telephones. They have stopped meeting in public. Many of them live right down underground. The report gives many other facts concerning them. I am just doubtful that the minister has put such an additional number of mounted police into the fight against communism in Canada as would be necessary to counter-balance the increased number which the F.B.I. have put into the fight against communism in the United States. If he has done so, well and good. I do not ask him to tell us. But if he has not done so, I would suggest that he had better take steps to increase the mounted police force in order to give them a fighting chance.
With regard to propaganda, I wonder whether the minister has read the book "While you Slept" by John T. Flynn, published in 1951, if I remember the date correctly. "While You Slept" is an account of the way in which the American people were softened up to the loss of China and how China was consequently thrown away by the United States into the hands of Russia. The betrayal was achieved by certain agents within the United States, including Owen Lattimore, Edgar Snow, Dean Acheson and several others. The whole story is given concerning the articles they wrote, the books they wrote, the criticisms of books they made and all the various other devices whereby the whole United States people were deceived concerning China until it was too late and China was gone, with 400 million people. There is not anything that the minister could read with greater profit than that book. If he has not read "The Iron Curtain Over America" I suggest that he read that book with great thoroughness, because it shows exactly the same thing that Flynn showed, only with much more extensive documentation. It contains unanswerable evidence showing the kind of techniques which are being employed by the communists in the cold war in order to achieve their objectives. I just wanted to mention that in passing.
I should now like to go a little bit further into the communist techniques in the cold war, coming a little bit closer to our own selves and what is happening to us just now.
There is a man in the United States, Professor Louis Francis Budenz who is, I presume, one of the greatest authorities on communism in America, a man who was himself in high command in the communist party, a man who was himself editor of the communist Daily Worker, who discontinued his

At that time I read to the house a list of typical goods which were being affected by this legislation, and I mentioned various things about it. Among these I referred to printed acetate foulard piece goods. The question was asked by the hon. member for Calgary North.
At this time in connection with the estimates of the Department of National Revenue I would answer the hon. member's question

in this way: This case is a typical illustration of the effect of the section. An importation of acetate foulard piece goods was made on February 22, 1954. The invoice price to the importer was 65 cents per yard. The goods had been originally introduced to their home market around May, 1953, at a price of 85 cents per yard. From May, 1953 to the date of the importation the price on the home market declined gradually from 85 cents to 65 cents, the price paid by the importer. The officers of the department, on examining the invoices, felt that investigation was necessary in accordance with our instructions which I read to the house on Friday, and personal investigation was accordingly made in the United States at the office of the exporter. This investigation provided the department with the volume of sales made on the home market and the prices prevailing during the six months immediately preceding the date of shipment to Canada, as is required by the act as amended last December.
As a result, the appraised value was set at 74-45 cents per yard. The difference, therefore, in the price to the importer and the appraised value on which duty and taxes were applied was the difference between 65 cents and 74*45 cents, that is, 9-45 cents.
Without the same elaboration as I have given in this case, I will refer to one or two other similar instances, one concerning a different type of textile, another one concerning refrigerators.
An importation on March 23 of over 100 pairs of drapes was invoiced at $6 per pair. These drapes, over the six months immediately preceding shipment to Canada, had dropped in price from $8.25 to $5 a pair. Following investigation by the department, the goods were appraised at $6.64 per pair, an increase in value for duty of 64 cents a pair.
Another typical example relates to the importation of household refrigerators entered at customs on February 22 last. This particular model was invoiced at $154.50. Investigation on the home market showed that during the six months immediately prior to shipment, the price had dropped from $179.70 to $163.70. After investigation the weighted average price over these six months was determined as being $178.48 which, under the law, is the appraised value for purposes of applying duties and taxes.

For some years now it has been my custom to make a few preliminary comments regarding the taxation division's estimates so that hon. members might be assisted in their consideration of these figures.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: I believe that these few brief remarks have brought out the more important factors in connection with the estimates of the taxation division, but I shall be glad to provide any additional information that hon. members may require.

I am grateful for the minister's statement which gives us a great many relevant facts. He has drawn our attention to various satisfactory features. I noticed with approval that advertising and travelling expenses were down. I do not propose to go in detail into the further figures which the minister has given because he has given us an adequate statement. I want to spend just a few minutes in talking about what I will call the spirit of the administration of the act because it is very important.
The minister has already indicated that a very large percentage of our whole taxation, roughly three-fifths, is derived from income tax. I think he said $2,600 million odd, about 50 per cent corporation and 50 per cent personal. The view is almost universally held now that the tax is a fair one; that the right basis of taxation is to pay according to ability to pay. It is rather ironical for me to recall that in a certain city in Canada in the 1920's the board of trade passed a resolution to the effect that they approved of the principle of income tax. There were two contrary expressions of opinion which reached me regarding that. One of my friends said: "Why did you not pass a resolution that the telephone was a useful thing?" But other people at that time were very indignant that the income tax had been approved by a responsible body of men. I mention that merely to indicate how opinion has moved in those years.
What I want to say about the act is that there are really two attitudes toward it. One is that certain types of citizens employ clever lawyers to enable them to evade the intent of the act. The other is that the act is administered in a heartless way in certain cases, quite contrary to common sense, and therefore contrary to what must have been the intention of parliament. I propose to give one or two illustrations for the minister's consideration, but I want to stress for a moment those two contrary attitudes.
I hold in my hand an interesting article on the income tax which appeared in the "Canadian Chartered Accountant" for April. It quotes at some length from a British case in which Lord Simon, the then lord chancellor, referred rather critically to citizens who were inclined to employ clever lawyers who he suggested were trying to evade the intent of the act. On the other hand, the writer of this article goes on to state the other side

and to say that there are cases where the government seeks to place interpretations on the provisions of the act which are both inequitable and diametrically opposed to ordinary legitimate business practices. I want to dwell on that just for a moment because it seems to me that it is very important to try to get our minds clear on that.
On the one hand, there is nothing I detest more than the person who manages to evade his just tax and thereby puts burdens on other people. Therefore, one wants vigilance on the part of the department. On the other hand, I am equally sure that one wants fairness, because there is the type of mind, there is the type of person who, if he is able to convince himself that the act is not administered fairly, then regards himself as quite justified in practising any evasion which he is able to practise. Therefore I say that we want vigilance and fairness, and I propose to bring to the minister's attention a few instances, seeking to explore this situation and to satisfy ourselves as far as we can in the short time which can be available for this discussion at this time, that the two are fairly held in balance.
The minister has given us a good deal of evidence of vigilance. We have had some complaints as to the method in which vigilance has been manifested and I propose to bring to the minister's attention one or two cases where I think vigilance, or perhaps vigilance plus an extreme interpretation in the courts, seemed to be in a fair way to work injustice.
I believe that that has been corrected by statute, in one instance I want to give, viz. the averaging of farm income. I believe that has been corrected by an amendment to the statute. But I want to read briefly the effect of the legal interpretation, which I believe was the accepted law for a time, because it seems to me to show that there is a danger for legalism to run riot. The description of this case I shall read now, and then comment further on it:
In the series of cases arising from the administration's attitude on the proper interpretation of section 39(1), we have the courts placed in the humorous position of deciding that ''parliament's intention" was that if a farmer did not file all of his tax returns in the averaged period on time, he was not entitled to average. I doubt very much if anyone, knowing parliament's attitude towards farmers, would seriously contend that that was parliament's intention. Can you imagine parliament passing on that section if the Minister of Finance, or someone for him, had said at the time, "This section means that any farmer who has failed by inadvertence to file one of the returns of the five averaged years on time being late by so much as one day, may lose thousands of dollars of tax refund, while at the same time remaining subject to the normal penalties for late filing, which parliament has previously decided were fair punishment for the offence"?

The point I stress is that here is a case where a penalty was provided by the act itself for failure to file a return and yet another surely unintended penalty was also exacted. I feel that this is contrary, not only to the words I read a moment ago, namely legitimate business practice, but so contrary to common sense that the Department of National Revenue should have taken immediate steps to have that set right by legislation if necessary. speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I think I can clear up this whole matter. As a matter of fact I promised to give an answer to the hon. member for Calgary North when he discussed the matter of farm assessment earlier in the session. I have given very careful thought to the subject, and I think if I were to put this statement on the record-it will only take a few minutes-it might answer many of the questions that have been asked and would be an answer to some of the criticism. May I put in on the record without reading it? If not, I will take the time to read it.
In view of recent critical statements made in the house and elsewhere with respect to the taxation division's assessing and investigation methods, particularly in dealing with farmers, a few general remarks in this connection may help to clarify our position.
In order to bring my remarks into proper perspective, I should like to state some of the things which are well known to all hon. members and which must be borne in mind when considering the income tax.
The majority of the citizens of this country honestly and conscientiously pay their proper taxes. There is, however, a minority who, not having enjoyed the opportunity of much formal education, do not understand the income tax law, or are not capable of correctly calculating their tax liability. There are still others, unfortunately, who resent having to pay their taxes and who take every means to avoid or evade the payment of their proper liability.
Now the majority who pay their taxes depend on the activities of my officers in the taxation division to discover those who have not paid and to make these delinquents aware of their obligations and to ensure that they pay their share of the cost of their government. This does not apply to farmers only;
6598	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Revenue it applies to taxpayers in all walks of life. Farmers are one group in the community and they must receive the attention of my officers in the same way as all other groups. I am sure that no person would suggest that the farmers should be overlooked or ignored.
It has been again suggested that farmers in some parts of the country have been singled out for discriminatory attention as compared with those elsewhere. Hon. members may recall my statement of March 12, 1952, Hansard page 361, refuting previous criticisms of this type, and pointing out the hazards inherent in attempting to use averages and broad generalizations of statistical data prepared for one purpose to establish specific conclusions for other purposes. At that time I freely admitted that our officers, being human, occasionally made mistakes, but they were honest mistakes which they were most anxious to rectify when they became apparent. I do not propose to embark on a further review of what I said at that time, but I believe it is equally applicable today and my current remarks may be considered as a further development and clarification of the stand then taken.
There have been from time to time a variety of approaches used in checking farmers' returns, and other classes of returns, in different areas. Methods tried and found satisfactory in one district are adopted by, or adapted to, others. Methods found wanting are rejected. New methods are continually being developed. As is recognized in all types of checking, auditing or investigational work, improvement in methods is only achieved by the use of imagination and experiment. We cannot overlook the wide variation in types of farming in Canada, many of which require different checking methods.
As our experience broadens a certain amount of standardization in general methods is taking place. For example, in the past exception has been taken to the division's procedure in some prairie districts of making requests by mail for farmers to meet assessors at central points for the purpose of reviewing their income tax returns and supporting records. It was originally thought that this approach was both satisfactory to the farmers and most efficient from an administrative viewpoint. However, as a result of our experience it has been found preferable to have the assessors in the prairie districts call on farm taxpayers at their home addresses, unless individual circumstances make alternative arrangements more convenient to the farmer. It is unreasonable, however, to anticipate elimination of local variations found necessary to meet local conditions.

Representations have also been made respecting some of the techniques in general use, particularly the so-called "net worth" approach. It has been suggested that we either abandon this assessment basis completely in so far as farmers are concerned, or restrict the net worth period to one or two years.
Before dealing with these suggestions I would like to give the house some indication of the extent of the activities to which such violent objection has been taken in some quarters. As a result of a special survey made recently it has been ascertained that in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953 less than 6 per cent of farmers' returns filed with the offices serving the three prairie provinces were assessed on a net worth basis. Now, remember that, less than 6 per cent were on a net worth basis. In the same period those offices assessed about 5 per cent of the returns filed by all other unincorporated businesses on that basis. To my mind, these figures indicate that the number of cases in which it was necessary to resort to a net worth basis of assessment was not unduly large. While the percentage of net worth actions with respect to farm returns was slightly higher than for other businesses this can, I think, be accounted for by the fact that farmers as a class do not keep as good records of their income and expenses as other classes of taxpayers.
Perhaps a word or two of explanation on the basic principle on which net worth assessments are based will be helpful. A net worth computation of income is based on the premise that the increase in a person's net assets between two dates, added to the amount of money spent for personal and family purposes, represents his income for the intervening period from all sources. If this result is adjusted where necessary by deducting moneys received from non-taxable sources, such as inheritance, gifts, or other capital gains, and by adding thereto any losses of a capital nature, we arrive at the income subject to tax. This principle is recognized as sound from an accounting viewpoint, and has been accepted on numerous occasions by the courts.
Hon. members should appreciate that an assessor does not resort to the comparative net worth basis of assessment as a matter of choice. He would much prefer to base the assessment on the taxpayer's actual income as disclosed by complete and accurate day-to-day records. However where there are no records or the records are shown to be incomplete and serious discrepancies in the taxpayer's returns cannot be reconciled

with known facts, the assessment must be made on the best information available. Under these circumstances the net worth approach is often the only reasonably accurate method remaining for the assessor to use in determining the taxpayer's income. It is used under similar conditions for all classes of taxpayers.
There has been critical comment on the fact that our assessors ask certain personal questions in compiling their statements which, it is suggested, have nothing to do with income tax. I assure you such questions are not an expression of idle curiosity on the part of the assessors. It must be obvious that one cannot determine a person's expenditure for food, clothing, recreation, furniture, education of children, medical bills, and the many other items entering into his family cost of living, without asking personal questions. Nor can one ascertain the assets or liabilities at certain dates, or the source and amounts of non-taxable income received, without asking such questions. We must not overlook the fact that these questions are directed as often as not to ascertaining facts of direct benefit to the taxpayer. In one recent case there was criticism of the fact that an assessor questioned the amount and use made of an ex-serviceman's gratuities. I believe that criticism was made by the hon. member for Calgary North. The fact is that the assessor was endeavouring to establish the amount of capital gain he could deduct from the veteran's income subject to tax.
An argument frequently encountered is that farmers generally have neither the time nor the education to keep proper records. All taxpayers in business, or who pay or collect taxes, are required by law to keep sufficiently detailed records to permit accurate determination of their net incomes. It has never been suggested that complicated formal accounting records are necessary for the average farmer, but he should keep a simple day-to-day record of his business transactions affecting revenue and expense. To exempt farmers from the responsibility of keeping records, or from net worth determination of income where necessary, or to drastically curtail the period applicable, could only be interpreted as unwarranted discrimination against other classes of taxpayers.
The advocates of such restrictions in the division's activities contend that, having once accepted a return without question or investigation, the division is showing bad faith in going back at some future date to reopen a return. This seems to resolve itself into an argument that if the taxpayer succeeds in an understatement or wilful suppression of income, or fails to keep accurate records
Supply-National Revenue without immediate detection, the division should be forever barred from collection of the proper tax. I assure you that we have resisted and will continue to resist such suggestions.
There are, I believe, adequate legal safeguards to prevent the authorities from unreasonable zeal in this matter of reassessment. I quote from subsection 4 of section 46 of the Income Tax Act:
(4) The minister may at any time assess tax, interest or penalties and may
(a)	at any time, if the taxpayer or person filing the return has made any misrepresentation or committed any fraud in filing the return or supplying information under this act, and
(b)	within 6 years from the day of an original assessment in any other case,
reassess or make additional assessments.
It will be noted that while the division's authority to assess or reassess is unlimited in the event of misrepresentation or fraud, a six-year limit is provided in all other cases.
A brief outline of our administrative methods illustrating the practical effect of our policies will indicate that this six-year general limit is not unreasonably long. The Canadian system of taxation is one of selfassessment and the taxpayer is required to make a return of his income and calculate his tax. In order to give proper service in such matters as the issuance of notices of assessment and the payment of refunds, as well as to improve the over-all administration of the division, we have in recent years subjected all returns to a rapid examination at the time of filing and, after correction of obvious errors, issued assessment notices almost immediately, acknowledging payments received and showing balances apparently owing or refunds of indicated overpayments. This phase of the program has met with almost unanimous public approval.
It is obviously necessary, however, as time and staff permit, to re-examine some of these returns. Methods of selection used vary but such considerations as complexity or scale of operation of the taxpayer, the necessity to check discrepancies, or the discovery of errors or omissions not previously discernible, all play their part. It may be said that all adjustments should be completed on the first examination, but when one reflects that over four million returns were filed in 1952, it will be evident that this could be done only by sacrificing the objective of prompt handling noted above, or by the use of an abortively large untrained seasonal staff, with a consequent loss of assessing quality, not to mention revenue. An important consideration is also the fact that errors of returns, particularly sustained suppressions of

Supply-National Revenue income, are frequently only apparent on concurrent examination of several years' returns of the same taxpayer. This is not feasible at a time when most of our district offices' daily intake of returns may number in the hundreds or thousands.
The re-examination of returns is therefore an orderly, continuous process throughout the year, interrupted to a limited degree by diversion of sufficient regular staff during the peak filing season to supervise and assist a comparatively small temporary clerical staff employed for that period to complete the first recording and examination of returns. I am satisfied that the relatively small but well trained permanent staff we now have employed under the present system is preferable, both from an efficiency and economy viewpoint, to the possible alternatives available.
Another frequently misunderstood phase of income tax administration is enforcement. It has doubtless come to the attention of many members that we sometimes find it necessary to take punitive legal action under the act. All classes of taxpayers have on occasion been prosecuted for failure to file returns of income, or for filing fraudulent returns. Such actions are invariably only initiated after the most careful review of all circumstances by senior officials of the division. The Income Tax Act, like any other law of vital importance to the national revenue, contains provisions necessary to its enforcement, but I can assure the house that the penalties provided are used only in cases involving refusal of taxpayers to comply with reasonable requests for returns or other information, or where wilful tax evasion is established.
We are keenly aware of the importance of good public relations in the difficult task of tax collection, and much has been done by way of radio and newspaper publicity, and through the medium of departmental publications, such as the farmer's and fisherman's guide, to explain our functions and requirements to the taxpaying public. I feel, however, that our best public relations medium is the day-to-day contact of our staff with the public, and all officers of the division are instructed to use the utmost tact and courtesy in their duties. In exercising their combined functions of collection and enforcement the psychological difficulties encountered cannot be overlooked, as it is too much to expect a tax collector to be welcomed with open arms. Consequently, we must expect some complaints-indeed the relatively small number is gratifying-but we cannot permit these complaints to curtail the legitimate and vitally necessary activities of the division.


We are glad to look into all reasonable objections raised, but we ask the co-operation of the public, their advisers, organized trade groups, and the members of this house in ensuring the representations made are reasonable in the light of all relevant facts.
I am sorry to take up so much of the time of the house in putting on the record this information, but I think it will be very useful to hon. members particularly in explaining methods which we use in the taxation branch. We are open at all times to suggestions from members of parliament with reference to giving a better service and guaranteeing revenues to the crown.

The situation in Quebec is a different thing. That has to be understood. We have heard that complaint for years with reference to getting after farmers in Alberta and in Saskatchewan. The raising of wheat in these prairie provinces is an industry. In the province of Quebec farming is a way of life, where they raise big families and they do not have any income tax to pay.

I have one question about the distribution of forms. It has been suggested to me that not sufficient forms get to certain post offices. Can the minister indicate in a word the system which is used in distributing forms?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We engage what may be called professionals to do that for us and pay them a fee, and they use the post offices as a distributing centre. It costs the government $420,000 a year to have these forms printed. In order that there might be a better distribution we engage a firm-I have forgotten the name for the moment-and pay them a fee, and they look after the distribution. In most communities they are distributed either through the taxation office, if there is one in the community, or through the local post office in smaller places. Anybody who cannot procure them that way can drop a letter to the department and they are sent to them.

About half way down page 371 I notice that there is a chauffeur added to the staff who was not there last year. Does that mean that some officer has grown in status to the point that he is entitled to a chauffeur, or is it a general utility one?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: I think we are too frugal in that. We have one automobile for the whole of Canada in the taxation division, and that is in Montreal.
